style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#29629B;--ltx-fill-color:#29629B;--ltx-fg-color:#29629B;\" color=\"#29629B\" fill=\"#29629B\" stroke=\"#29629B\" stroke-width=\"2.5pt\"><path style=\"fill:none\" d=\"M 1.73 156.24 L 1.73 0\"></path></g><g fill-opacity=\"1.0\" transform=\"matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 15.56 142.14)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:40.85em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"12.3\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)\" width=\"565.25\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS5.p5.pic1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:40.85em;\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS5.p5.pic1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.SS5.p5.pic1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif ltx_font_bold\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#25588C;\">Lesson: Prefer empirical threshold tuning over first-principles calculation</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity=\"1.0\" transform=\"matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 15.56 14.1)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:44.93em;--ltx-fo-height:7.95em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"112.7\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 110.01)\" width=\"621.7\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS5.p5.pic1.2\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:44.93em;\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS5.p5.pic1.2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.SS5.p5.pic1.2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#000000;\">The specific values for caps (context pressure thresholds, pruning protection windows, reminder frequencies, iteration limits) resist first-principles calculation. They depend on the interaction between model behavior, typical user workflows, and system overhead in ways that are difficult to predict. Starting with conservative values and tuning based on observed failure modes (sessions that compact too early, reminders that fire too often, loops that run too long) is more effective than attempting to derive optimal values analytically. In our system, the 70% compaction trigger, 3 nudge attempts, and 6 thinking depth levels all emerged from iterative failure analysis.</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Self-healing indexes.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Caching frequently-accessed metadata in a lightweight index file enables fast listing without scanning underlying data files (<a href=\"#S2.SS5.SSS1\" title=\"2.5.1 Session Storage ‣ 2.5 Persistence Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.5.1</span></a>). If the index is missing or corrupted, automatically rebuilding it from the underlying data makes the index a performance optimization rather than a single point of failure. The same principle applies to any derived data structure: design it so that loss triggers regeneration, not failure.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Deterministic operations outside the agent loop.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Not everything needs to go through the agent. Session management, mode switching, model selection, and server configuration are deterministic operations that should be handled directly at the input boundary (via slash-prefix dispatch or equivalent) with no approval gates, no undo tracking, and no token cost (<a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS4\" title=\"2.2.4 REPL Command Dispatch ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.4</span></a>). Routing these through the LLM wastes context and introduces unnecessary nondeterminism.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">These five design tensions (context as a budget, behavioral steering over long horizons, safety through architectural constraints, designing for approximate outputs, and bounding unbounded growth) are not unique to <span id=\"S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span>. They reflect fundamental challenges in building any long-running agentic system. The following section surveys how the broader research community has approached these same challenges, positioning <span id=\"S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span>’s design decisions within the evolving landscape of code intelligence, autonomous software engineering, and context engineering.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_section\">4 </span>Related Work</h2>\n\n<div id=\"S4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The development of terminal-centric AI coding agents draws upon a rich and rapidly evolving body of work spanning code intelligence, autonomous software engineering, and interactive agent design. In this section, we survey the key research streams that inform our system design and contextualize <span id=\"S4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> within the broader landscape.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S4.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">4.1 </span>Code Generation and Code LLMs</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The application of LLMs to programming has progressed from function-level generation, benchmarked by HumanEval <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib15\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">15</a>]</cite> and MBPP <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib6\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">6</a>]</cite>, through class-level tasks such as ClassEval <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib23\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">23</a>]</cite>, to repository-level challenges that demand cross-file planning and multi-step reasoning <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib47\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">47</a>]</cite>. Specialized code LLMs including DeepSeek-Coder <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib33\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">33</a>]</cite>, StarCoder <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib48\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">48</a>]</cite>, CodeLlama <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib72\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">72</a>]</cite>, and CodeT5+ <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib87\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">87</a>]</cite> have driven this progression, supported by unified toolkits such as CodeTF <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib11\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">11</a>]</cite> that standardize training and inference across models, while Retrieval-Augmented Generation <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib44\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">44</a>]</cite> and reinforcement learning address the gap between isolated generation and realistic repository-scale tasks <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib47\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">47</a>]</cite>. <span id=\"S4.SS1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> builds on this foundation by embedding code LLMs within an agentic loop that provides the navigation, editing, and execution capabilities necessary to apply generated code in real repositories.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">4.2 </span>Autonomous Issue Resolution</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">SWE-bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib40\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">40</a>]</cite> defined the task of autonomous issue resolution, catalyzing a research frontier that spans single-agent, multi-agent, and workflow-based approaches <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite>. Single-agent frameworks such as SWE-Agent <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib94\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">94</a>]</cite> pioneered autonomous file navigation and code editing, while AutoCodeRover <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib108\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">108</a>]</cite> and HyperAgent <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib69\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">69</a>]</cite> extended this to iterative refinement and generalist task solving. Multi-agent systems distribute the problem across specialized roles: MAGIS <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib78\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">78</a>]</cite> assigns role-playing collaboration, CodeR <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib14\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">14</a>]</cite> introduces task-graph execution, and platforms such as OpenHands <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib84\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">84</a>]</cite> orchestrate heterogeneous agents through ensemble selection <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite>. Workflow-based approaches like Agentless <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib89\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">89</a>]</cite> enforce structured pipelines (localization, repair, validation) for improved reproducibility.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS2.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Beyond architectural choices, the community has explored both training-based and inference-time methods to improve agent capabilities. Supervised fine-tuning with curriculum learning <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib91\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">91</a>]</cite> and synthetic data <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib68\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">68</a>]</cite>, combined with RL algorithms leveraging process-oriented rewards <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib53\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">53</a>]</cite>, equip models with stronger issue-resolution skills. At inference time, Monte Carlo Tree Search <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib112\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">112</a>]</cite> enables flexible backtracking over repair trajectories, while parallel exploration strategies such as CodeMonkeys <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib86\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">86</a>]</cite> maximize solution coverage <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite>. <span id=\"S4.SS2.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> draws on these advances, combining single-agent autonomy with structured subagent delegation and workflow-based safety enforcement. Across these paradigms, agents increasingly rely on code itself as their primary medium of reasoning and action.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS3\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">4.3 </span>Code as a Core Medium for Generalist Agents</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Recent work has highlighted a paradigm shift from pure natural language reasoning to code-driven agent interactions <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib47\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">47</a>]</cite>. Using code as a universal medium gives agents precise tool invocation, reproducible state management, and composable action primitives.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Interaction protocols.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Standardized tool-use patterns such as ReAct <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib99\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">99</a>]</cite> and ReWOO <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib92\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">92</a>]</cite> enable precise tool invocation and state management. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib1\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">1</a>]</cite> introduces structured message formats for reliable multi-turn tool orchestration, while multi-agent coordination schemes such as Agent-to-Agent (A2A) enable direct inter-agent communication <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib47\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">47</a>]</cite>.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Thinking and acting in code.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><em id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Reasoning methods</em> such as Program-Aided Language Models (PAL) <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib27\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">27</a>]</cite>, Program-of-Thoughts <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib47\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">47</a>]</cite>, and Chain-of-Code <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib47\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">47</a>]</cite> enable LLMs to generate and execute code for structured reasoning. <em id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Action execution</em> frameworks translate plans into runnable code: CodeAct <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib83\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">83</a>]</cite> enables interactive operations through executable Python, TaskWeaver <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib71\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">71</a>]</cite> converts requests into plugin-based function calls, and CodeAgents <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib77\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">77</a>]</cite> provides additional orchestration patterns. <em id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Domain applications</em> extend this paradigm beyond software engineering, from healthcare (EHRAgent <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib36\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">36</a>]</cite>) to robotic control (Code as Policies <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib52\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">52</a>]</cite>).</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Memory with code.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Code-based storage strategies have proven effective for managing LLM context constraints. Voyager <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib81\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">81</a>]</cite> stores validated skills as executable code for later reuse, while Reasoning Bank <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib54\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">54</a>]</cite> enables rule-based learning from repair trajectories. MemGPT <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib66\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">66</a>]</cite> and ExpeRepair <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib106\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">106</a>]</cite> introduce hierarchical and dual-memory architectures for context management, both discussed further in the context engineering subsection below.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">By operating within terminal environments and embracing execution feedback through shell commands, OpenDev directly aligns with the “Acting in Code” philosophy, leveraging the shell as a universal interpreter to orchestrate complex, multi-step workflows.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS4\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">4.4 </span>Agentic Software Engineering Workflows</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Agentic Software Engineering formalizes the workflows through which human engineers and LLMs collaborate on software tasks. Hassan et al. <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib35\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">35</a>]</cite> provide a comprehensive research roadmap that identifies foundational pillars including agent orchestration, environment design, and lifecycle management.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Iterative and prompt-driven workflows.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The Plan–Do–Assess–Review (PDAR) loop formalizes a single task’s lifecycle: planning through Product Requirement Prompts (PRPs), implementation by a dev-agent, self-assessment, and human review <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib35\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">35</a>]</cite>. CLI toolkits such as SuperClaude template these loops for consistency and convenience, but stop short of a team-level methodology.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Spec-driven development.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">A growing family of frameworks treats structured specifications, rather than source code, as the primary source of truth for AI-assisted development. GitHub’s Spec Kit <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib31\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">31</a>]</cite> introduces a four-phase workflow (Specify, Plan, Tasks, Implement) where a formal <span id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">spec.md</span> and optional <span id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">constitution.md</span> govern every agent-driven change, ensuring that AI-generated code aligns with explicitly declared intent and architectural constraints. OpenSpec <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib26\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">26</a>]</cite> takes a complementary brownfield-first approach, designed for evolving existing codebases rather than greenfield projects: each proposed change generates spec deltas (ADDED/MODIFIED/REMOVED requirements in GIVEN/WHEN/THEN format) against a persistent specification baseline, making modifications auditable before any code is written. Both frameworks are agent-agnostic, integrating with 17+ coding assistants via slash commands and filesystem conventions rather than tool-specific APIs.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Multi-agent and agile-inspired frameworks.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">BMAD <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib9\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">9</a>]</cite> takes the team metaphor further by organizing agents into agile roles (Product Owner, Architect, Developer, Scrum Master, Tester), with PRDs and story files enabling parallel execution across isolated Git branches <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib35\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">35</a>]</cite>. A key architectural decision is work sharding: the Scrum Master agent decomposes tasks into self-contained story files, each carrying exactly the context a Developer agent needs, which addresses context-window limitations by design rather than through compression. A crucial delineation in the broader SASE roadmap proposes separating workspaces into an Agent Command Environment (ACE) for human supervision and orchestration, and an Agent Execution Environment (AEE) for scalable agent operations <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib35\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">35</a>]</cite>.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Mentorship and lifecycle management.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The SASE roadmap <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib35\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">35</a>]</cite> introduces the concept of Mentorship-as-Code, where review feedback becomes version-controlled, testable MentorScript rules, enabling cumulative improvement across tasks. Agent lifecycle management shifts agents from stateless contractors to persistent teammates with memory, observability, and secure execution.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> embodies the characteristics of an execution-focused terminal hub, bridging iterative development cycles natively via command-line interactivity and treating command outputs as direct signals for autonomous debugging and loop refinement.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS5\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">4.5 </span>Agent Tool Systems and Modular Components</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In training-free frameworks, LLMs rely on specialized tools to augment reasoning without fine-tuning. These tools are organized along the repair pipeline: bug reproduction, fault localization, code search, patch generation, validation, and test generation <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite>.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS5.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS5.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Bug reproduction tools like AEGIS <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib51\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">51</a>]</cite> provide automated environment setup and reproduction workflows, ensuring consistent execution contexts. Fault localization tools include Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) and graph-based methods that construct code dependency graphs <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite>. Code search tools range from interactive retrieval using BM25 and AST-based APIs to graph-based understanding via Knowledge Graphs and Language Server Protocols <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib58\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">58</a>, <a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite>. Patch generation tools employ robust editing formats (e.g., AutoDiff) and ensemble selection through regression testing <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite>. SpecRover <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib16\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">16</a>]</cite> uses specification-guided search for high-quality patches. Test generation tools such as Otter <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib109\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">109</a>]</cite> and Issue2Test <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib82\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">82</a>]</cite> use feedback-driven mechanisms to synthesize failing tests that reproduce reported defects <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite>.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS5.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS5.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S4.SS5.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> adopts a registry-based tool architecture with lazy discovery, hierarchical skill templates, and defense-in-depth safety mechanisms, balancing comprehensive capability with token efficiency.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS6\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">4.6 </span>Context Engineering for Long-Horizon Agents</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS6.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS6.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Context management is a fundamental challenge for long-running agent systems. Issue resolution tasks often require long-horizon, multi-turn interaction that raises both API cost and performance degradation from context rot <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite>.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Formal foundations and taxonomy.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Mei et al. <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib56\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">56</a>]</cite> provide the first comprehensive survey of context engineering (CE) for LLMs, formalizing the context supplied to a model as a structured tuple <math id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"C=\\mathcal{A}(c_{\\text{instr}},c_{\\text{know}},c_{\\text{tools}},c_{\\text{mem}},c_{\\text{state}},c_{\\text{query}})\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒜</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>instr</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>know</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>tools</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>mem</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>state</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>query</mtext></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">C=\\mathcal{A}(c_{\\text{instr}},c_{\\text{know}},c_{\\text{tools}},c_{\\text{mem}},c_{\\text{state}},c_{\\text{query}})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{A}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math> is an assembly function that orchestrates instructional context, external knowledge, tool schemas, memory, execution state, and the user query. The survey organizes the field around three pillars: <em id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">context retrieval</em> (selecting relevant information from external sources), <em id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">context processing</em> (transforming, compressing, or restructuring retrieved content), and <em id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">context management</em> (maintaining coherence and relevance across turns). <span id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span>’s architecture maps directly onto this taxonomy: its prompt composer assembles <math id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"c_{\\text{instr}}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>instr</mtext></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">c_{\\text{instr}}</annotation></semantics></math> from modular markdown sections, the tool registry manages <math id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"c_{\\text{tools}}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>tools</mtext></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">c_{\\text{tools}}</annotation></semantics></math> with lazy MCP discovery, the memory pipeline maintains <math id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"c_{\\text{mem}}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>mem</mtext></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">c_{\\text{mem}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and adaptive compaction handles <math id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"c_{\\text{state}}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>state</mtext></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">c_{\\text{state}}</annotation></semantics></math> across long sessions.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Historical and theoretical perspective.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Hua et al. <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib39\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">39</a>]</cite> situate context engineering within a broader intellectual history, tracing four eras of development: early prompt engineering focused on single-turn instruction, retrieval-augmented generation that introduced external knowledge, tool-augmented agents that expanded the action space, and the current CE 2.0 era that treats context as a first-class engineering concern. Drawing on Dey’s formal definition of context from ubiquitous computing and Weiser’s vision of calm technology, they articulate three guiding principles: <em id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">entropy reduction</em> (each context element should reduce uncertainty about the desired output), <em id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">minimal sufficiency</em> (include only what is necessary to avoid attention dilution), and <em id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">semantic continuity</em> (context should evolve coherently across turns rather than being reconstructed from scratch). They also identify a narrowness gap in current systems, which overwhelmingly focus on chat history management while neglecting holistic context dimensions such as tool state, environmental signals, and cross-session knowledge. <span id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span>’s system reminders, which inject event-driven context at attention-critical positions, directly address the semantic continuity principle, while its staged compaction implements entropy reduction by progressively summarizing low-value history.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px3\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Context processing and compression techniques.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The survey literature documents substantial quantitative gains from structured context processing <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib56\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">56</a>]</cite>. Chain-of-thought variants (tree-of-thought <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib98\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">98</a>]</cite>, graph-of-thought <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib8\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">8</a>]</cite>) improve multi-step reasoning by structuring intermediate context, while compression methods reduce token costs without proportional quality loss: the In-context Autoencoder <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib29\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">29</a>]</cite> achieves 4<math id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\times\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\times</annotation></semantics></math> compression, and PREMISE reduces prompt length by 87.5% while preserving task performance. On the retrieval side, Self-RAG <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib5\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">5</a>]</cite> introduces self-reflective retrieval that adaptively decides when to retrieve and critiques its own outputs, RAPTOR <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib73\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">73</a>]</cite> builds recursive tree-structured summaries for hierarchical retrieval, and GraphRAG leverages knowledge graph structures (e.g., HippoRAG <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib34\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">34</a>]</cite>) to improve retrieval precision for complex queries. These advances reveal a fundamental asymmetry: LLMs are more robust to compressed context during understanding tasks than during generation tasks, suggesting that aggressive compression is most viable for context that informs reasoning rather than context that directly shapes output text. <span id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span>’s compaction strategy exploits this asymmetry by aggressively summarizing tool outputs and historical turns (understanding context) while preserving system instructions and recent user messages (generation context) verbatim.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Meta-level context optimization.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Ye et al. <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib101\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">101</a>]</cite> introduce Meta Context Engineering (MCE), a framework that treats context engineering itself as an optimization problem rather than a manual design task. They formalize the agent’s context as a bi-level optimization: the outer loop searches over context configurations (system prompts, tool schemas, memory strategies) while the inner loop evaluates agent performance on downstream tasks. A key insight is that fixed evaluation harnesses introduce systematic bias into agent benchmarks, as the harness itself shapes the context in ways that may advantage certain strategies over others. MCE addresses this by co-evolving the agent’s context and evaluation setup using a <math id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"(1{+}1)\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">(1{+}1)</annotation></semantics></math>-ES with crossover, an evolutionary strategy that mutates and recombines context configurations. On SWE-bench Verified, MCE achieves 89.1% resolve rate compared to 70.7% for the hand-engineered baseline, while also being 13.6<math id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\times\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster due to more efficient context utilization. The optimized configurations transfer across tasks, suggesting that meta-learned context strategies capture general principles rather than task-specific artifacts. This line of work implies that hand-designed context engineering, including the strategies employed by <span id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span>, could eventually be complemented or replaced by learned optimization of context assembly.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Memory integration empowers agents to transcend isolated problem-solving by accumulating historical context. Approaches range from hierarchical storage separating general knowledge from repository-specific details <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite>, to cognitive architectures that partition knowledge into episodic, semantic, and procedural stores <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib56\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">56</a>, <a href=\"#bib.bib111\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">111</a>, <a href=\"#bib.bib38\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">38</a>]</cite>. Building on the memory primitives discussed above (MemGPT’s virtual paging <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib66\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">66</a>]</cite>, ExpeRepair’s dual-memory <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib106\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">106</a>]</cite>), more recent work explores population-level memory: agent variant populations <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib17\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">17</a>]</cite> maintain diverse exploration histories for robust decision-making, while experience banks <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib85\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">85</a>]</cite> guide search through accumulated knowledge. Current frontiers prioritize distilling transferable reasoning strategies, shifting from storing raw data to abstracting high-level policies from trajectories <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite>.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Memory-driven scaling approaches complement the inference-time strategies discussed above by integrating persistent context to reduce redundant exploration, enabling agents to build on past attempts rather than starting fresh. Context compression for long-horizon agents has seen notable advances: ACON <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib41\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">41</a>]</cite> optimizes compression policies for extended agent sessions, while Context-Folding <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib76\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">76</a>]</cite> scales agent capabilities through recursive context summarization. At the frontier, Agentic Context Engineering <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib107\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">107</a>]</cite> enables models to evolve their own contexts through self-improvement loops. Multi-agent communication has matured through a progression of standardized protocols, from early knowledge-sharing languages (KQML, FIPA ACL) to modern interoperability standards including MCP <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib1\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">1</a>]</cite> for tool integration, Agent-to-Agent (A2A) for direct inter-agent messaging, and Agent Communication Protocol (ACP) for structured multi-agent coordination <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib56\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">56</a>]</cite>. <span id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> addresses these challenges through automatic compaction that preserves critical information while summarizing history, combined with dual-memory architecture and template-based error recovery. Young <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib102\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">102</a>]</cite> formalizes the notion of an agent <em id=\"S4.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p3.1.2\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">harness</em> as the runtime framework that coordinates these concerns (tool dispatch, context lifecycle, progress tracking, and clean handoffs between context windows) for agents operating over extended timeframes.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS7\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">4.7 </span>Benchmarks for Evaluating Agentic Coding Systems</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS7.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS7.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Having introduced foundational code generation benchmarks above, we focus here on the evaluation ecosystem around agentic systems. The scope of benchmarks has progressively widened: from function- and class-level generation (APPS <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib37\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">37</a>]</cite>, CodeContests <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib50\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">50</a>]</cite>), through repository-level issue resolution anchored by SWE-bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib40\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">40</a>]</cite> and its variants (SWE-bench Verified <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib64\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">64</a>]</cite>, Multi-SWE-bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib104\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">104</a>]</cite>, SWE-bench Multimodal <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib96\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">96</a>]</cite>, SWE-bench Pro <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib21\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">21</a>]</cite>, SWE-Lancer <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib59\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">59</a>]</cite>), to environment-grounded interaction tasks such as WebArena <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib113\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">113</a>]</cite>, OSWorld <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib90\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">90</a>]</cite>, and EnvBench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib24\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">24</a>]</cite>. Complementary benchmarks target specific dimensions: SWT-Bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib60\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">60</a>]</cite> for testing workflows, FEA-Bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib49\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">49</a>]</cite> for feature implementation, NL2Repo-Bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib22\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">22</a>]</cite> for repository generation, DevEval <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib45\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">45</a>]</cite> for the full development lifecycle, and SWE-EVO <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib79\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">79</a>]</cite> for long-horizon software evolution.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS7.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS7.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Specialized benchmarks evaluate capabilities beyond general code editing. <math id=\"S4.SS7.p2.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\tau\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\tau</annotation></semantics></math>-Bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib97\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">97</a>]</cite> and the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib67\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">67</a>]</cite> assess tool-use and function-calling proficiency. In scientific and ML engineering, ReplicationBench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib100\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">100</a>]</cite> targets research replication, MLGym <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib61\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">61</a>]</cite> and MLE-Bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib12\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">12</a>]</cite> evaluate ML research and engineering tasks, and CORE-Bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib75\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">75</a>]</cite> measures computational reproducibility. For long-horizon terminal interaction, Terminal-Bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib57\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">57</a>]</cite> demonstrates that frontier agents resolve fewer than 65% of curated CLI tasks, while LongCLI-Bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib25\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">25</a>]</cite> finds pass rates below 20% for multi-category programming tasks spanning development, feature addition, bug fixing, and refactoring.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS8\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">4.8 </span>Evaluation Methodology and Best Practices</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS8.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS8.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Rigorous evaluation of agentic systems requires careful benchmark design beyond simple accuracy metrics. The Agentic Benchmark Checklist <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib114\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">114</a>, <a href=\"#bib.bib115\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">115</a>]</cite> formalizes best practices including clear task definition, reproducibility guarantees, contamination prevention, and efficiency-aware metrics. LLM-as-Judge approaches such as MT-Bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib110\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">110</a>]</cite> enable scalable quality assessment when traditional metrics fail to capture semantic correctness, though data contamination remains a critical concern requiring continuous benchmark renewal <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib93\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">93</a>, <a href=\"#bib.bib20\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">20</a>]</cite>. Efficiency metrics (API costs, inference time, and token consumption <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib55\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">55</a>]</cite>) and long-task completion measurement <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib42\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">42</a>, <a href=\"#bib.bib43\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">43</a>]</cite> provide holistic assessment of agent practicality for real-world deployment.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS9\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">4.9 </span>Human–Agent Collaboration</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S4.SS9.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS9.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">LongCLI-Bench provides compelling evidence that human–agent collaboration significantly improves task completion. Static plan injection, where key plans are provided before execution, outperforms self-correction in both pass rate and efficiency. Dynamic interactive guidance, where agents request human intervention based on their current state, achieves even higher performance. The combined setting yields the best results while reducing the need for human intervention <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib25\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">25</a>]</cite>. These findings strongly indicate that rather than exclusively pursuing full autonomy, future systems should develop collaborative workflows that leverage synergy between efficient agent execution and human strategic guidance. <span id=\"S4.SS9.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> supports this paradigm through its approval workflows, interactive command execution, and structured feedback loops.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS9.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS9.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The research landscape surveyed above reveals a clear trajectory: from isolated code generation toward integrated, long-horizon agent systems that must balance capability, safety, and context efficiency. The benchmarks increasingly demand sustained multi-step reasoning in realistic environments, while the methods progressively address the engineering challenges (context management, tool orchestration, memory, and safety) that such sustained operation requires. The following section synthesizes the specific future directions that emerge from the intersection of <span id=\"S4.SS9.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span>’s architectural experience and these broader research trends.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S5\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_section\">5 </span>Conclusion and Future Directions</h2>\n\n<div id=\"S5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This paper presented <span id=\"S5.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span>, an open AI-powered command-line agent for software engineering, and documented the architectural decisions, design trade-offs, and lessons learned from building a production-ready system. Key contributions include a compound AI system architecture <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib103\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">103</a>]</cite> with multi-model routing (<a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS5\" title=\"2.2.5 Workload-Optimized Multi-Model Architecture ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.5</span></a>), an extended ReAct pipeline with thinking and critique phases (<a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS6\" title=\"2.2.6 Extended ReAct Execution Loop ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.6</span></a>), Adaptive Context Compaction (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS6\" title=\"2.3.6 Adaptive Context Compaction ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.6</span></a>), event-driven system reminders (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS4\" title=\"2.3.4 Context-Aware System Reminders ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.4</span></a>), an experience-driven memory pipeline, lazy tool discovery via MCP (<a href=\"#S2.SS4.SSS7\" title=\"2.4.7 Token-Efficient External Tool Discovery via MCP ‣ 2.4 Tool System ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.4.7</span></a>), and a dual-interface abstraction.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The central architectural insight is that per-workflow LLM binding (<a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS5\" title=\"2.2.5 Workload-Optimized Multi-Model Architecture ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.5</span></a>) yields model-agnosticity: adapting to new models requires only configuration changes, not code changes. Schema-level safety enforcement (<a href=\"#S2.SS2\" title=\"2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2</span></a>) proved more robust than runtime permission checks, as removing write tools from the planning agent’s schema eliminates an entire class of bypass attempts. Conditional prompt composition (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS1.Px2\" title=\"Mode-specific variants and variable substitution. ‣ 2.3.1 Dynamic System Prompt Construction ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.1</span></a>) reduced overhead by excluding irrelevant instructions while preserving comprehensive guidance when needed. On the context engineering side, managing the finite context window emerged as a first-class engineering concern rather than a secondary optimization. Adaptive Context Compaction (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS6\" title=\"2.3.6 Adaptive Context Compaction ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.6</span></a>), which transitions observations through active, faded, and archived states, reduced peak context consumption by approximately 54% and often eliminated the need for emergency summarization. The three-tier context architecture (static system prompt, dynamic just-in-time reminders (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS4\" title=\"2.3.4 Context-Aware System Reminders ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.4</span></a>), and long-horizon persistence) addressed the attention-decay problem where agents reliably violated instructions after 30+ tool calls. The Agentic Context Engineering memory pipeline enables the agent to learn from tool outcomes within and across sessions without hardcoding strategies into prompts.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The cross-cutting design tensions and transferable lessons that emerged from this work are synthesized in <a href=\"#S3\" title=\"3 Discussion ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">3</span></a>, which examines context pressure as a first-class constraint, behavioral steering over long horizons, safety through architectural enforcement rather than runtime checks, tool design that absorbs LLM imprecision, and resource bounding strategies for long-running sessions.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Several capabilities previously identified as future work, such as per-step undo via shadow git snapshots (<a href=\"#S2.SS5.SSS2\" title=\"2.5.2 Operation Log and Undo ‣ 2.5 Persistence Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.5.2</span></a>), has been implemented during continued development, demonstrating the extensibility of the layered architecture.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.p5\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.p5.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Several promising research directions emerge from the challenges identified in this work:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.p6\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<ul id=\"S5.p6.1\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"S5.I1.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S5.I1.i1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S5.I1.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.I1.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Quantitative evaluation on established benchmarks.</span> This paper documents architectural decisions and design rationale but lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Benchmarking on SWE-bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib95\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">95</a>]</cite>, Terminal-Bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib57\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">57</a>]</cite>, and LongCLI-Bench <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib25\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">25</a>]</cite>, part of the broader evaluation ecosystem surveyed in <a href=\"#S4\" title=\"4 Related Work ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a>, would validate the architecture against established baselines and identify specific improvement areas. Terminal-Bench’s finding that frontier agents resolve fewer than 65% of tasks, and LongCLI-Bench’s observation that pass rates remain below 20% for long-horizon tasks, suggest substantial room for improvement in context management and multi-step reasoning.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S5.I1.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S5.I1.i2.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S5.I1.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.I1.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Adaptive resource allocation.</span> Current parameters - the 70% compaction threshold, 3 nudge attempts, 6 thinking depth levels - are globally fixed. Adaptive approaches that dynamically adjust based on task complexity, current context pressure, and error history could optimize the cost–quality–latency triangle per task rather than relying on one-size-fits-all constants. For instance, a simple debugging task should skip the thinking phase entirely, while a complex architectural refactoring may benefit from deeper deliberation and a more conservative compaction strategy.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S5.I1.i3\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S5.I1.i3.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S5.I1.i3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.I1.i3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S5.I1.i3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Scaling the memory pipeline.</span> The ACE playbook currently operates per-project with effectiveness scoring and semantic retrieval. Cross-project knowledge transfer - where lessons learned in one repository inform behavior in similar projects - hierarchical bullet organization that separates general programming heuristics from project-specific conventions, and active learning that selectively requests user feedback on uncertain bullets could substantially improve the agent’s ability to accumulate and apply experience over time.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S5.I1.i4\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S5.I1.i4.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S5.I1.i4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.I1.i4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S5.I1.i4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Structured code representations for memory.</span> The current memory pipeline stores experience as flat natural-language bullets. Richer representations, such as code dependency graphs that capture relationships between modules, call graphs that track function interactions, and project-level ontologies that encode domain concepts, could enable more precise retrieval and reasoning. Combining graph-structured code understanding with long-term persistent memory that spans not just sessions but entire project lifecycles would allow the agent to build deep, evolving models of codebases rather than accumulating isolated observations.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S5.I1.i5\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S5.I1.i5.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S5.I1.i5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.I1.i5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S5.I1.i5.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Multi-agent coordination beyond hierarchical delegation.</span> Current subagents execute independently under main-agent coordination, communicating only through completion markers. Richer coordination patterns - peer-to-peer communication between subagents, shared blackboard architectures for collaborative problem-solving, and negotiation protocols for resolving conflicting tool outcomes - could enable more sophisticated workflows such as concurrent code review and implementation, or parallel exploration with result synthesis.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S5.I1.i6\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S5.I1.i6.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S5.I1.i6.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.I1.i6.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S5.I1.i6.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Learned system reminder optimization.</span> The 24-template reminder catalog and its injection timing were manually engineered based on observed failure modes. Automated discovery of effective reminder patterns - through reinforcement learning on attention-decay metrics, learned injection timing based on conversation dynamics, or adaptive template selection conditioned on agent state - could improve nudge effectiveness while reducing the manual engineering burden of designing and maintaining reminder templates.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S5.I1.i7\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S5.I1.i7.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S5.I1.i7.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S5.I1.i7.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S5.I1.i7.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Hybrid CLI–IDE integration.</span> The dual-interface architecture demonstrates that a shared callback protocol can serve fundamentally different frontends. Extending this to IDE plugins - where the same agent logic powers both terminal workflows and rich editor integration - would serve users who want visual affordances (inline diffs, symbol navigation, test result overlays) alongside terminal autonomy, without duplicating agent logic across environments.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.p7\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.p7.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Building effective agentic coding systems requires navigating competing concerns: capability versus complexity, autonomy versus safety, generality versus token efficiency. The design space is rich with trade-offs where no single choice dominates. We hope that the architectural patterns, engineering lessons, and candid reflections on what worked and what did not, documented in this paper, help future builders of agentic systems make more informed decisions as they navigate these choices.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"bib\" class=\"ltx_bibliography\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_bibliography\">References</h2>\n\n<ul
