class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:429/87;\" width=\"429\" height=\"87\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 3: </span>Visualization of a trace segment in <span id=\"S3.F3.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span>. This illustrates an agent-to-agent conversation exhibiting Failure Mode 2.4: Information Withholding. The Phone Agent fails to communicate API requirements (username format) to the Supervisor Agent, who also fails to seek clarification, leading to repeated failed logins and task failure.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S3.SS4\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">3.4 </span>Constructing the Multi-Agent Dataset</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Before large-scale data collection for <span id=\"S3.SS4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span>, we confirm the generalizability of our finalized <span id=\"S3.SS4.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> and the LLM annotator. We evaluate their performance on two new MAS (OpenManus and Magentic-One) with two new benchmarks (MMLU and GAIA, the latter representing a new general-agent task domain for validation) not part of the initial <span id=\"S3.SS4.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> development. An additional human IAA round on these out-of-domain traces using the finalized <span id=\"S3.SS4.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> yields a strong Cohen’s Kappa score of 0.79. This demonstrates <span id=\"S3.SS4.p1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>’s effectiveness in capturing failures in diverse systems and tasks without further modification, supporting the robustness of our annotation approach for broader application. We further detail the uniqueness of <span id=\"S3.SS4.p1.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> failure modes via a correlation study in Appendix <a href=\"#A5\" title=\"Appendix E MAS Failure Modes Correlation ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">E</span></a>.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.SS4.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS4.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Leveraging our validated <span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> and LLM annotator, we expand data collection to construct <span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span>, comprising 1642 annotated traces from seven popular MAS frameworks (Table <a href=\"#S1.T1\" title=\"Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">1</span></a>). These frameworks include the five from our initial studies, the two from the generalization validation, and Manus <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib45\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">45</a>]</cite> as detailed in Appendix <a href=\"#A2\" title=\"Appendix B Details of Multi-Agent Systems Evaluated ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">B</span></a>. These traces cover diverse tasks like coding, math problem-solving, and general agent functionalities. For <span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span>, our LLM annotator identifies <span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> failure modes in each trace and provides a corresponding reason. We also release <span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data-human</span>, consisting of all traces annotated by human experts during our IAA studies, where each annotation specifies <span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> failure modes with textual justifications. We open-source <span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.1.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> and <span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.1.8\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data-human</span> as resources to analyze MAS failure dynamics and guide robust system design.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_section\">4 </span>The Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy</h2>\n\n<div id=\"S4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This section details <span id=\"S4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>, a key result of our study and a critical component that guides the creation and analysis of <span id=\"S4.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span>. <span id=\"S4.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> provides the first empirically grounded, structured framework for defining, understanding, and annotating common failures in MAS. Here, we present its structure, the failure categories it defines, and key insights derived from its development and application.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S4.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S4.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>, illustrated in Figure <a href=\"#S0.F1\" title=\"Figure 1 ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">1</span></a>, identifies 14 fine-grained failure modes, which we map to MAS execution stages (Pre-Execution, Execution, and Post-Execution) where their root causes commonly emerge. These modes are organized into 3 overarching categories reflecting the fundamental nature of the observed failures. While we recognize that prior works have noted some individual failure types and we do not claim <span id=\"S4.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> is exhaustive, it offers precise definitions for a structured approach to understanding why MAS fail. Detailed definitions for each failure mode (FM) are available in Appendix <a href=\"#A1\" title=\"Appendix A MAST Failure Categories: Deep Dive ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">A</span></a>, with specific examples in Appendix <a href=\"#A14\" title=\"Appendix N Examples of Different Failure Modes ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">N</span></a>.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S4.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We acknowledge that some MAS failures can stem from fundamental limitations of current LLMs, such as hallucination or instruction following. However, in developing <span id=\"S4.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>, we focus on identifying failure patterns where improvements in system design, agent coordination, and verification can offer room to improve the reliability of MAS, often independently of or complementary to advancements in the base models themselves. We now discuss each failure category (FC) in <span id=\"S4.p3.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> and its implications.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\"><span class=\"ltx_inline-block\"><svg id=\"S4.p4.pic1\" class=\"ltx_picture\" height=\"124.52\" overflow=\"visible\" version=\"1.1\" viewBox=\"0 0 477.38 124.52\" width=\"477.38\"><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;\" fill=\"#000000\" stroke=\"#000000\" stroke-width=\"0.4pt\" transform=\"translate(0,124.52) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)\"><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#002676;\" fill=\"#002676\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0 5.91 L 0 118.62 C 0 121.88 2.64 124.52 5.91 124.52 L 471.47 124.52 C 474.73 124.52 477.38 121.88 477.38 118.62 L 477.38 5.91 C 477.38 2.64 474.73 0 471.47 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#F2F4F8;\" fill=\"#F2F4F8\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 118.62 C 1.97 120.79 3.73 122.56 5.91 122.56 L 471.47 122.56 C 473.65 122.56 475.41 120.79 475.41 118.62 L 475.41 5.91 C 475.41 3.73 473.65 1.97 471.47 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z\"></path></g><g fill-opacity=\"1.0\" transform=\"matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.3 8.99)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:33.59em;--ltx-fo-height:7.89em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"111.93\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 109.24)\" width=\"464.79\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S4.p4.pic1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:33.59em;\">\n<span id=\"S4.p4.pic1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S4.p4.pic1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#000000;\">FC1. System Design Issues.<span id=\"S4.p4.pic1.1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_medium\"> Failures originate from system design decisions, and poor or ambiguous prompt specifications.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\">\n<span id=\"S4.p4.pic1.1.1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block fa fa-lightbulb-o\" aria-hidden=\"true\">\n</span></span>. Insight 1.<span id=\"S4.p4.pic1.1.1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_medium\"> MAS failure is not merely a function of challenges in the underlying model; a well-designed MAS can result in performance gain when using the same underlying model.</span></span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.p5\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S4.p5.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Failures in FC1 occur during execution but often reflect flaws in pre-execution design choices regarding system architecture, prompt instructions, or state management. These include failing to follow task requirements (FM-1.1, 11.8%) or agent roles (FM-1.2, 1.5%), step repetitions (FM-1.3, 15.7%), context loss (FM-1.4, 2.80%), or not recognizing task completion (FM-1.5, 12.4%). While FM-1.1 and FM-1.2, disobey specifications, may seem like general instruction-following limitation, we identify deeper causes: (1) flaws in MAS design regarding agent roles and workflow, (2) poor user prompt specifications, or (3) limitations of the underlying LLM. We posit that a well-designed MAS should interpret high-level objectives with minimal but clear user input to mitigate the impact of points (2) and (3).</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.p6\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S4.p6.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">For instance, when ChatDev is tasked to create a Wordle game with the prompt <span id=\"S4.p6.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_italic\">a standard wordle game by providing a daily 5-letter...</span>, the generated program uses a fixed word dictionary. Even with a more explicit prompt like <span id=\"S4.p6.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_italic\">...without having a fixed word bank, and randomly select a new 5-letter word each day</span>, ChatDev still produces code with a fixed list and new errors. This suggests failures stem from the MAS’s design for interpreting specifications. Our intervention studies (Appendix <a href=\"#A8\" title=\"Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">H</span></a>) show that improving agent role specifications alone yields a +9.4% success rate increase for ChatDev with the same user prompt and LLM (GPT-4o).</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.p7\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\"><span class=\"ltx_inline-block\"><svg id=\"S4.p7.pic1\" class=\"ltx_picture\" height=\"124.52\" overflow=\"visible\" version=\"1.1\" viewBox=\"0 0 477.38 124.52\" width=\"477.38\"><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;\" fill=\"#000000\" stroke=\"#000000\" stroke-width=\"0.4pt\" transform=\"translate(0,124.52) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)\"><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#002676;\" fill=\"#002676\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0 5.91 L 0 118.62 C 0 121.88 2.64 124.52 5.91 124.52 L 471.47 124.52 C 474.73 124.52 477.38 121.88 477.38 118.62 L 477.38 5.91 C 477.38 2.64 474.73 0 471.47 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#F2F4F8;\" fill=\"#F2F4F8\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 118.62 C 1.97 120.79 3.73 122.56 5.91 122.56 L 471.47 122.56 C 473.65 122.56 475.41 120.79 475.41 118.62 L 475.41 5.91 C 475.41 3.73 473.65 1.97 471.47 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z\"></path></g><g fill-opacity=\"1.0\" transform=\"matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.3 8.99)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:33.59em;--ltx-fo-height:7.89em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"111.93\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 109.24)\" width=\"464.79\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S4.p7.pic1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:33.59em;\">\n<span id=\"S4.p7.pic1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S4.p7.pic1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#000000;\">FC2. Inter-Agent Misalignment.<span id=\"S4.p7.pic1.1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_medium\"> Failures arise from a breakdown in critical information flow from inter-agent interaction and coordination during execution. \n<br class=\"ltx_break\">\n<span id=\"S4.p7.pic1.1.1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block fa fa-lightbulb-o\" aria-hidden=\"true\">\n</span></span>. Insight 2.<span id=\"S4.p7.pic1.1.1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_medium\"> Solutions focused on context or communication protocols are often insufficient for FC2 failures, which demand deeper ‘social reasoning’ abilities from agents.</span></span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.p8\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S4.p8.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FC2 covers failures in agent coordination. These include unexpected conversation resets (FM-2.1, 2.20%), proceeding with wrong assumptions instead of seeking clarification (FM-2.2, 6.80%), task derailment (FM-2.3, 7.40%), withholding crucial information (FM-2.4, 0.85%), ignoring other agents’ input (FM-2.5, 1.90%), or mismatches between reasoning and action (FM-2.6, 13.2%). Figure <a href=\"#S3.F3\" title=\"Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Enabling Scalable Annotation: The LLM-as-a-Judge Pipeline ‣ 3 The Multi-Agent Systems Dataset ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">3</span></a> illustrates information withholding (FM-2.4). Diagnosing FC2 failures can be complex, as similar surface behaviors (e.g., missing information) can stem from different root causes like withholding (FM-2.4), ignoring input (FM-2.5), or context mismanagement (FM-1.4), underscoring the need for <span id=\"S4.p8.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>’s fine-grained modes.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.p9\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S4.p9.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Recent system innovations, such as Model Context Protocol <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">46</a>]</cite> and Agent to Agent <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib47\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">47</a>]</cite>, improve agent communication by standardizing message formats from different tool or agent providers. However, the errors we observe in FC2 occur even when agents within the same framework communicate using natural language. This signals a deeper agent interaction dynamic challenge: the collapse of ’theory of mind’ <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib48\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">48</a>]</cite>, where agents fail to accurately model other agents’ informational needs. Addressing this likely requires structural improvements to the content of agent messages or enhancing models’ contextual reasoning and their capacity to infer other agents’ informational needs, such as through targeted training, as base LLMs are generally not pre-trained for such nuanced inter-agent dynamics. Thus, robust solutions will likely involve a combination of improved MAS architecture and model-level advancements in communicative intelligence.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.p10\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\"><span class=\"ltx_inline-block\"><svg id=\"S4.p10.pic1\" class=\"ltx_picture\" height=\"107.92\" overflow=\"visible\" version=\"1.1\" viewBox=\"0 0 477.38 107.92\" width=\"477.38\"><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;\" fill=\"#000000\" stroke=\"#000000\" stroke-width=\"0.4pt\" transform=\"translate(0,107.92) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)\"><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#002676;\" fill=\"#002676\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0 5.91 L 0 102.01 C 0 105.28 2.64 107.92 5.91 107.92 L 471.47 107.92 C 474.73 107.92 477.38 105.28 477.38 102.01 L 477.38 5.91 C 477.38 2.64 474.73 0 471.47 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#F2F4F8;\" fill=\"#F2F4F8\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 102.01 C 1.97 104.19 3.73 105.95 5.91 105.95 L 471.47 105.95 C 473.65 105.95 475.41 104.19 475.41 102.01 L 475.41 5.91 C 475.41 3.73 473.65 1.97 471.47 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z\"></path></g><g fill-opacity=\"1.0\" transform=\"matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.3 8.99)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:33.59em;--ltx-fo-height:6.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"95.32\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 92.63)\" width=\"464.79\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S4.p10.pic1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:33.59em;\">\n<span id=\"S4.p10.pic1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S4.p10.pic1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#000000;\">FC3. Task Verification.<span id=\"S4.p10.pic1.1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_medium\"> Failures involve inadequate verification processes that fail to detect or correct errors, or premature termination of tasks.\n\n<br class=\"ltx_break\">\n<span id=\"S4.p10.pic1.1.1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block fa fa-lightbulb-o\" aria-hidden=\"true\">\n</span></span>. Insight 3.<span id=\"S4.p10.pic1.1.1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_medium\"> Multi-Level Verification is Needed. Current verifier implementations are often insufficient; sole reliance on final-stage, low-level checks is inadequate.</span></span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.p11\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S4.p11.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FC3 failures are related to the quality control of the final output, including premature termination (FM-3.1, 6.20%), no or incomplete verification (FM-3.2, 8.20%), or incorrect verification (FM-3.3, 9.10%). These highlight challenges in ensuring output correctness and reliability. Systems with explicit verifiers like MetaGPT and ChatDev generally show fewer total failures (Figure <a href=\"#S5.F4\" title=\"Figure 4 ‣ 5 Towards better Multi-Agent LLM Systems ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a>), indicating explicit checks help. However, the presence of a verifier is not a silver bullet, as overall MAS success rates can still be low. For example (FM-3.2), a ChatDev-generated chess program passes superficial checks (e.g., code compilation) but contains runtime bugs because it fails to validate against actual game rules, rendering the output unusable despite review phases.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.p12\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S4.p12.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">During our GT analysis of MAS traces, we find that many existing verifiers perform only superficial checks, despite being prompted to perform thorough verification, such as checking if the code compiles or if there are leftover <span id=\"S4.p12.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_italic\">TODO</span> comments. We posit that MAS development should take lessons from traditional software development where programmers test their code before committing. More rigorous verification is needed, such as using external knowledge, collecting testing output throughout generation, and multi-level checks for both low-level correctness and high-level objectives. We demonstrate this in an intervention study where adding a high-level task objective verification step to ChatDev yields a +15.6% improvement in task success on ProgramDev (details in Appendix <a href=\"#A8\" title=\"Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">H</span></a>).</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S5\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_section\">5 </span>Towards better Multi-Agent LLM Systems</h2>\n\n<figure id=\"S5.F4\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><object type=\"image/svg+xml\" data=\"2503.13657v3/masft_bar.svg\" id=\"S5.F4.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:452/182;\" width=\"452\" height=\"182\"></object>\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 4: </span>Distribution of failure in <span id=\"S5.F4.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> with <span id=\"S5.F4.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> labels on total 210 traces. This plot visualizes the failure distributions of the first 30 traces for each system. As the specific tasks and benchmarks may differ across the MAS configurations shown, these results are intended to illustrate system-specific failure profiles rather than to serve as a performance comparison across MAS.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<div id=\"S5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We now discuss the broader implications and usage of <span id=\"S5.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> and <span id=\"S5.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>. <span id=\"S5.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span>, with its annotations grounded in <span id=\"S5.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>, provides crucial empirical evidence, while <span id=\"S5.p1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> offers a foundational framework and practical tool for understanding, debugging, and ultimately improving MAS. By concretely defining failure modes and providing a large-scale dataset of their occurrences, our work outlines the challenges in building reliable MAS and opens targeted research problems for the community.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S5.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">5.1 </span>Failure Breakdown in <span id=\"S5.SS1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span></h3>\n\n<div id=\"S5.SS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S5.SS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Our analysis of <span id=\"S5.SS1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> reveals that failure distributions differ markedly across various MAS, often reflecting their unique architectural characteristics and design philosophies. For example, as illustrated in Figure <a href=\"#S5.F4\" title=\"Figure 4 ‣ 5 Towards better Multi-Agent LLM Systems ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a>, we observe specific patterns: AppWorld frequently suffers from premature terminations (FM-3.1), potentially due to its star topology and lack of a predefined workflow making termination conditions less obvious; OpenManus exhibits a tendency towards step repetition (FM-1.3); and HyperAgent could benefit from addressing its dominant failure modes of step repetition (FM-1.3) and incorrect verification (FM-3.3). These system-specific profiles underscore that there is no one-size-fits-all solution to MAS failures.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.SS1.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S5.SS1.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We also use <span id=\"S5.SS1.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> to study the impact of different underlying language models and MAS designs on failure patterns. For instance, when comparing GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 Sonnet within the MetaGPT framework on programming tasks, we find that while GPT-4o generally performs better than Claude, it shows significantly fewer FC1 (System Design Issues) failures by 39%. We also examine the impact of different MAS designs on the same benchmark, such as comparing MetaGPT and ChatDev on ProgramDev. Here, while MetaGPT generally outperforms ChatDev by having 60-68% less failure in FC1 and FC2, it has 1.56x more FC3 failure than ChatDev. These comparative analyses, detailed further in Appendix <a href=\"#A6\" title=\"Appendix F Understanding Failures: The Impact of Different LLMs and Agent Architectures ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">F</span></a>, provide insights into how model choice and architectural patterns influence system performance and distribution of failures.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S5.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">5.2 </span><span id=\"S5.SS2.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> as a Practical Development Tool</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S5.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S5.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Developing robust MAS is challenging: aggregate success rates can obscure the specific impacts of optimizations. <span id=\"S5.SS2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> addresses this by providing a structured vocabulary for systematic failure breakdown. Using our LLM annotator with <span id=\"S5.SS2.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>, developers can obtain quantitative analyses of failure profiles for specific systems. We demonstrate <span id=\"S5.SS2.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>’s practical usage in guiding MAS improvement in our case studies (Appendix <a href=\"#A8\" title=\"Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">H</span></a>). The Failure Mode breakdown analysis (Appendix <a href=\"#A8.SS3\" title=\"H.3 Effect of the interventions on MAST ‣ Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">H.3</span></a>) shows which failure modes were mitigated and reveals any resulting trade-offs. This granular view, moving beyond aggregate metrics, is crucial for understanding <span id=\"S5.SS2.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">why</span> an intervention works and for iterating effectively towards more robust systems.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S5.SS3\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">5.3 </span>Beyond Model Capabilities: The Primacy of System Design</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S5.SS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S5.SS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">While one could simply attribute failures in <span id=\"S5.SS3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> to limitations of present-day LLM (e.g., hallucinations, misalignment), we conjecture that improvements in the base model capabilities will be insufficient to address the full <span id=\"S5.SS3.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>.\nInstead, we argue that good MAS design requires organizational understanding – even organizations of sophisticated individuals can fail catastrophically <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib49\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">49</a>]</cite> if the organization structure is flawed. Previous research in high-reliability organizations has shown that well-defined design principles can prevent such failures <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib50\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">50</a>, <a href=\"#bib.bib51\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">51</a>]</cite>.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.SS3.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S5.SS3.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Consistent with organization theories, our findings indicate that many MAS failures arise from the challenges in organizational design and agent coordination rather than the limitations of individual agents. In our intervention case studies (Appendix <a href=\"#A8\" title=\"Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">H</span></a>), we apply MAS system workflow and prompt changes respectively (results in Table <a href=\"#A8.T5\" title=\"Table 5 ‣ H.2 Case Study 2: ChatDev ‣ Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">5</span></a>). With the same underlying model, we achieve max improvements of 15.6%. This highlights that MAS failures can be address with better system designs.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.SS3.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S5.SS3.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Although first step interventions lead to performance gains, not all failure modes are resolved, and task completion rates still remain low, indicating that more substantial improvements are needed. Achieving high reliability may requires combinatorial changes ranging from agent system organization to model level improvements (see Table <a href=\"#A7.T4\" title=\"Table 4 ‣ G.2 Structural Strategies ‣ Appendix G Approaches and strategies to improve MASs ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a>). <span id=\"S5.SS3.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>, by providing a clear framework of failure points identified from <span id=\"S5.SS3.p3.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span>, helps identify where these structural weaknesses lie and can guide the design and evaluation of more sophisticated MAS architectures.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S6\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_section\">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>\n\n<div id=\"S6.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In this study, we conduct the first systematic investigation into why MAS fail. This investigation results in the <span id=\"S6.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span>: a comprehensive public resource of over 1600 annotated execution traces from 7 popular MAS frameworks, which we create to outline MAS failure dynamics and guide future system development. To enable <span id=\"S6.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span>’s systematic annotation and analysis, we first develop the <span id=\"S6.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">M</span>ulti-<span id=\"S6.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">A</span>gent <span id=\"S6.p1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">S</span>ystem Failure <span id=\"S6.p1.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">T</span>axonomy (<span id=\"S6.p1.1.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>). We build <span id=\"S6.p1.1.8\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> through a rigorous Grounded Theory-based analysis of an initial 150 traces, validating its definitions with strong inter-annotator agreement and identifying 14 distinct failure modes across 3 categories. For scalable annotation of <span id=\"S6.p1.1.9\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> using <span id=\"S6.p1.1.10\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>, we then develop an LLM annotator, confirming its high agreement with human experts. Together, <span id=\"S6.p1.1.11\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> and <span id=\"S6.p1.1.12\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> provide a foundational framework and empirical grounding for future MAS research.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S6.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We are excited about the potential of MAS, but their widespread adoption hinges on achieving greater reliability. Our work, through the public release of <span id=\"S6.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span>, <span id=\"S6.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>, and the LLM annotator, contributes towards this goal. <span id=\"S6.p2.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> offers a rich empirical basis for understanding current failure dynamics, while <span id=\"S6.p2.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> provides a standardized language and framework to diagnose and mitigate these failures. By systematically identifying and categorizing challenges, we aim to open up concrete research directions and equip the community to develop more robust and effective multi-agent systems.</p>\n</div>\n<div class=\"ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage\"></div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"bib\" class=\"ltx_bibliography\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_bibliography\">References</h2>\n\n<ul class=\"ltx_biblist\">\n      \n<li id=\"bib.bib1\" class=\"ltx_bibitem\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem\">[1]</span>\n<span class=\"ltx_bibblock\">\nLeo Tolstoy.\n\n</span>\n<span class=\"ltx_bibblock\"><em id=\"bib.bib1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Anna Karenina</em>.\n\n</span>\n<span class=\"ltx_bibblock\">The Russian Messenger, 1878.\n\n</span></li>\n      \n<li id=\"bib.bib2\" class=\"ltx_bibitem\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem\">[2]</span>\n<span class=\"ltx_bibblock\">\nShishir G. commented.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A1\" class=\"ltx_appendix\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix A </span><span id=\"A1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> Failure Categories: Deep Dive</h2>\n\n<section id=\"A1.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">A.1 </span>FC1. System Design Issues</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A1.SS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.SS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This category includes failures that arise from deficiencies in the design of the system architecture, poor conversation management, unclear task specifications or violation of constraints, and inadequate definition or adherence to the roles and responsibilities of the agents.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A1.SS1.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.SS1.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We identify five failure modes under this category:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A1.SS1.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<ul id=\"A1.I1\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"A1.I1.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I1.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I1.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-1.1: <span id=\"A1.I1.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Disobey task specification</span> - Failure to adhere to the specified constraints or requirements of a given task, leading to suboptimal or incorrect outcomes.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A1.I1.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I1.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I1.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-1.2: <span id=\"A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Disobey role specification</span> - Failure to adhere to the defined responsibilities and constraints of an assigned role, potentially leading to an agent behaving like another.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A1.I1.i3\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I1.i3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I1.i3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-1.3: <span id=\"A1.I1.i3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Step repetition</span> - Unnecessary reiteration of previously completed steps in a process, potentially causing delays or errors in task completion.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A1.I1.i4\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I1.i4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I1.i4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-1.4: <span id=\"A1.I1.i4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Loss of conversation history</span> - Unexpected context truncation, disregarding recent interaction history and reverting to an antecedent conversational state.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A1.I1.i5\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I1.i5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I1.i5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-1.5: <span id=\"A1.I1.i5.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Unaware of termination conditions</span> - Lack of recognition or understanding of the criteria that should trigger the termination of the agents’ interaction, potentially leading to unnecessary continuation.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A1.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">A.2 </span>FC2. Inter-Agent Misalignment</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A1.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This category includes failures arising from ineffective communication, poor collaboration, conflicting behaviors among agents, and gradual derailment from the initial task.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A1.SS2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.SS2.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We identify six failure modes under this category:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A1.SS2.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<ul id=\"A1.I2\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"A1.I2.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I2.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I2.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-2.1: <span id=\"A1.I2.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Conversation reset</span> - Unexpected or unwarranted restarting of a dialogue, potentially losing context and progress made in the interaction.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A1.I2.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I2.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I2.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-2.2: <span id=\"A1.I2.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Fail to ask for clarification</span> - Inability to request additional information when faced with unclear or incomplete data, potentially resulting in incorrect actions.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A1.I2.i3\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I2.i3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I2.i3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-2.3: <span id=\"A1.I2.i3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Task derailment</span> - Deviation from the intended objective or focus of a given task, potentially resulting in irrelevant or unproductive actions.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A1.I2.i4\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I2.i4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I2.i4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-2.4: <span id=\"A1.I2.i4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Information withholding</span> - Failure to share or communicate important data or insights that an agent possess and could impact decision-making of other agents if shared.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A1.I2.i5\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I2.i5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I2.i5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-2.5: <span id=\"A1.I2.i5.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Ignored other agent’s input</span> - Disregarding or failing to adequately consider input or recommendations provided by other agents in the system, potentially leading to suboptimal decisions or missed opportunities for collaboration.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A1.I2.i6\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I2.i6.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I2.i6.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-2.6: <span id=\"A1.I2.i6.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Reasoning-action mismatch</span> - Discrepancy between the logical reasoning process and the actual actions taken by the agent, potentially resulting in unexpected or undesired behaviors.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A1.SS3\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">A.3 </span>FC3. Task Verification</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A1.SS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.SS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This category includes failures resulting from premature execution termination, as well as insufficient mechanisms to guarantee the accuracy, completeness, and reliability of interactions, decisions, and outcomes.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A1.SS3.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.SS3.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We identify three failure modes under this category:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A1.SS3.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<ul id=\"A1.I3\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"A1.I3.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I3.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I3.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-3.1: <span id=\"A1.I3.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Premature termination</span> - Ending a dialogue, interaction or task before all necessary information has been exchanged or objectives have been met, potentially resulting in incomplete or incorrect outcomes.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A1.I3.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I3.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I3.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-3.2: <span id=\"A1.I3.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">No or incomplete verification</span> - (partial) omission of proper checking or confirmation of task outcomes or system outputs, potentially allowing errors or inconsistencies to propagate undetected.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A1.I3.i3\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A1.I3.i3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.I3.i3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">FM-3.3: <span id=\"A1.I3.i3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Incorrect verification</span> - Failure to adequately validate or cross-check crucial information or decisions during the iterations, potentially leading to errors or vulnerabilities in the system.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n<div class=\"ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage\"></div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A2\" class=\"ltx_appendix\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix B </span>Details of Multi-Agent Systems Evaluated</h2>\n\n<div id=\"A2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In this section, we provide details on MAS we evaluated during this study and their performance benchmark evaluation.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"A2.F5\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><object type=\"image/svg+xml\" data=\"2503.13657v3/multi_agent_systems_failure_rates.svg\" id=\"A2.F5.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square\" style=\"aspect-ratio:238/205;\" width=\"238\" height=\"205\"></object>\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 5: </span>Failure rates of six popular Multi-Agent LLM Systems with GPT-4o and Claude-3.7-Sonnet. Performances are measured on different benchmarks, therefore they are not directly comparable.\n</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<section id=\"A2.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">B.1 </span>Overview of MAS</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A2.SS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.SS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In this study, we evaluated 7 open-source frameworks. The architecture and the purpose of the systems is detailed in the table below.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"A2.T3\" class=\"ltx_table\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption\"><span class=\"ltx_tag id=\"A2.T3.4.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle\" style=\"width:79.7pt;\">\n<span id=\"A2.T3.4.1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_p ltx_align_center\"><span id=\"A2.T3.4.1.1.1.1.1\" open-source multi-agent framework designed to facilitate the development of collaborative AI agents that solve real-world tasks. It was inspired by the Manus AI agent.</span></span>\n</span></td></tr>\n</table>\n</figure>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A2.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">B.2 </span>Multi-Agent Systems in the Initial Annotation Phase</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A2.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A2.SS2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic\">MetaGPT.</span> MetaGPT <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib52\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">52</a>]</cite> is a multi-agent system that simulates a software engineering company and involves agents such as a Coder and a Verifier. The goal is to have agents with domain-expertise (achieved by encoding Standard Operating Procedures of different roles into agents prompts) collaboratively solve a programming task, specified in natural language.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A2.SS2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.SS2.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A2.SS2.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic\">ChatDev.</span>\nChatDev is a generalist multi-agent framework that initializes different agents, each assuming common roles in a software-development company <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib56\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">56</a>]</cite>. The framework breaks down the process of software development into 3 phases: design, coding and testing. Each phase is divided into sub-tasks, for example, testing is divided into code review (static) and system testing (dynamic). In every sub-task, two agents collaborate where one of the agents acts as the orchestrator and initiates the interaction and the other acts as an assistant to help the orchestrator achieve the task. The 2 agents then hold a multi-turn conversation to achieve the goal stated by the orchestrator ultimately leading to the completion of the task, marked by a specific sentinel by either agents. ChatDev has the following agent roles: CEO, CTO, Programmer, Reviewer and Tester. ChatDev introduces “Communicative Dehallucination”, which encourages the assistant to seek further details about the task over multiple-turns, instead of responding immediately.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A2.SS2.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.SS2.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A2.SS2.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic\">HyperAgent.</span>\nHyperAgent <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib53\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">53</a>]</cite> is a framework for software engineering tasks organized around four primary agents: Planner, Navigator, Code Editor, and Executor.\nThese agents are enhanced by specialized tools, designed to provide LLM-interpretable output.\nThe Planner communicates with child agents via a standardized message format with two fields: Context (background and rationale) and Request (actionable instructions).\nTasks are broken down into subtasks and published to specific queues.\nChild agents, such as Navigator, Editor, and Executor instances, monitor these queues and process tasks asynchronously, enabling parallel execution and significantly improving scalability and efficiency.\nFor example, multiple Navigator instances can explore different parts of a large codebase in parallel, the Editor can apply changes across multiple files simultaneously, and the Executor can run tests concurrently, accelerating validation.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A2.SS2.p4\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.SS2.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A2.SS2.p4.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic\">AppWorld.</span>\nAppWorld is a benchmark, that provides an environment with elaborate mocks of various everyday services like eShopping Website, Music Player, Contacts, Cost-sharing app, e-mail, etc <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib54\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">54</a>]</cite>. The benchmark consists of tasks that require executing APIs from multiple services to achieve the end-users tasks. The AppWorld benchmark provides a ReAct based agent over GPT-4o as a strong baseline. We create a multi-agent system over AppWorld derived from the baseline ReAct agent, where each agent specializes in using one of the services mocked in AppWorld, with detailed instructions about the APIs available in that service, and access to the documentation for that specific service. A supervisor agent receives the task instruction to be completed, and can hold one-on-one multi-turn conversations with each of the service-specific agents. The service-agents are instructed to seek clarification with the supervisor, whenever required. The supervisor agent holds access to various information about the human-user, for example, credentials to access various services, name, email-id and contact of the user, etc, which the service-agents need to access the services, and must clarify with the supervisor agent.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A2.SS2.p5\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.SS2.p5.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A2.SS2.p5.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic\">AG2.</span> AG2 (formerly AutoGen) <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib57\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">57</a>]</cite> is an open-source programming framework for building agents and managing their interactions.\nWith this framework, it is possible to build various flexible conversation patterns, integrating tools usage and customizing the termination strategy.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A2.SS3\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">B.3 </span>Closed-Source MAS</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A2.SS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.SS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In our efforts to build a comprehensive dataset, we also explore popular closed-source platforms that are speculated to function as MAS. A notable example is Manus <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib45\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">45</a>]</cite>, a general AI agent platform. However, evaluating and incorporating such systems into <span id=\"A2.SS3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> for fine-grained failure analysis presents significant challenges. Specifically, with systems like Manus, the underlying language model is often not disclosed, and more critically, the platforms may not provide access to full agent execution traces. This lack of transparency into the internal conversational and operational steps makes reliable, detailed failure annotation using <span id=\"A2.SS3.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> infeasible. While we conduct human evaluation of task correctness for some closed-source systems (for instance, Manus achieves a 60% success rate on our ProgramDev benchmark), the absence of comprehensive trace data prevents their inclusion in the primary <span id=\"A2.SS3.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> which focuses on deeply annotated failure dynamics. Our focus for <span id=\"A2.SS3.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span> thus remains on systems where such trace analysis can yield robust insights.</p>\n</div>\n<div class=\"ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage\"></div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A3\" class=\"ltx_appendix\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix C </span><span id=\"A3.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> Python Library</h2>\n\n<div id=\"A3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In order to ease the usage of <span id=\"A3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>, we also package our code as a pip installable python library, under the name <code id=\"A3.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter\">agentdash</code>. The example usage is shown below.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A3.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<div id=\"A3.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_listing ltx_lstlisting ltx_listing\"><div class=\"ltx_listing_data\"><a href=\"data:text/plain;base64,\" download=\"\">⬇</a></div>\n<div id=\"lstnumberx1\" class=\"ltx_listingline\"><span id=\"lstnumberx1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\" id=\"A4\" class=\"ltx_appendix\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix D </span>ProgramDev and ProgramDev-v2 Datasets</h2>\n\n<div id=\"A4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The ProgramDev dataset contains 30 coding problems <span id=\"footnote3\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">3</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">3</sup>\n            <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\">3</span>\n            \n            \n            \n            \n            \n            \n            \n          <a href=\"https://github.com/multi-agent-systems-failure-taxonomy/MAST/blob/main/traces/programdev/programdev_dataset.json\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter\">https://github.com/multi-agent-systems-failure-taxonomy/MAST/blob/main/traces/programdev/programdev_dataset.json</a></span></span></span>. These tasks are programming challenges, such as implementing Tic-Tac-Toe, Chess, or Sudoku, for which abundant solutions and descriptions are readily available online. We design ProgramDev with tasks intended to be relatively straightforward for MAS, rather than exceptionally difficult, to better isolate specific failure dynamics. We later extend this to ProgramDev-v2, a 100-problem dataset developed primarily for the comparative analyses of MAS architectures and underlying LLMs presented in Figure <a href=\"#A6.F8\" title=\"Figure 8 ‣ Appendix F Understanding Failures: The Impact of Different LLMs and Agent Architectures ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">8</span></a>.</p>\n</div>\n<div class=\"ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage\"></div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A5\" class=\"ltx_appendix\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix E </span>MAS Failure Modes Correlation</h2>\n\n<div id=\"A5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We evaluate <span id=\"A5.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>’s effectiveness based on three key aspects: its generalization to unseen systems and datasets, the balanced distribution of identified failures, and the distinctiveness of its failure categories. This section details the correlation analysis.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A5.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A5.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Figure <a href=\"#A5.F6\" title=\"Figure 6 ‣ Appendix E MAS Failure Modes Correlation ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">6</span></a> shows low correlations (0.17-0.32). This suggests that the categories capture distinct aspects of MAS failures with limited overlap, supporting the taxonomy’s structure. This distinctiveness is crucial because, as noted in Insight 2, failures with similar surface behaviors can stem from different root causes (e.g., memory management vs. agent coordination).</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A5.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A5.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Although <span id=\"A5.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>’s fine-grained nature helps differentiate root cause, it also poses a challenge for our LLM annotator. Analyzing correlations between specific failure modes (see Appendix <a href=\"#A5\" title=\"Appendix E MAS Failure Modes Correlation ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">E</span></a> for Figure <a href=\"#A5.F7\" title=\"Figure 7 ‣ Appendix E MAS Failure Modes Correlation ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">7</span></a>)\nshows moderate correlations (max of 0.63) between modes with similar symptoms might lead automated evaluators to conflate distinct root causes.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"A5.F6\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><img src=\"2503.13657v3/masft_fc_corr.png\" id=\"A5.F6.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square\" style=\"aspect-ratio:238/195;\" width=\"238\" height=\"195\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 6: </span>MAS failure modes correlation matrix</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<figure id=\"A5.F7\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><img src=\"2503.13657v3/masft_fm_corr.png\" id=\"A5.F7.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square\" style=\"aspect-ratio:333/301;\" width=\"333\" height=\"301\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 7: </span>MAS failure modes correlation matrix</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<div class=\"ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage\"></div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A6\" class=\"ltx_appendix\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix F </span>Understanding Failures: The Impact of Different LLMs and Agent Architectures</h2>\n\n<figure id=\"A6.F8\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><object type=\"image/svg+xml\" data=\"2503.13657v3/effect_of_underlying_llm_system_design.svg\" id=\"A6.F8.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:476/166;\" width=\"476\" height=\"166\"></object>\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 8: </span>Comparison on <span id=\"A6.F8.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> failure modes and categories on ProgramDev-v2 dataset explained in Section <a href=\"#A4\" title=\"Appendix D ProgramDev and ProgramDev-v2 Datasets ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">D</span></a> to analyze LLM choice effect. MetaGPT is used for both cases with GPT-4o and Claude-3.7-Sonnet on two comparative cases.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<figure id=\"A6.F9\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><object type=\"image/svg+xml\" data=\"2503.13657v3/effect_of_mas_architecture_system_design.svg\" id=\"A6.F9.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:476/166;\" width=\"476\" height=\"166\"></object>\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 9: </span>Comparison on <span id=\"A6.F9.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> failure modes and categories on ProgramDev-v2 dataset explained in Section <a href=\"#A4\" title=\"Appendix D ProgramDev and ProgramDev-v2 Datasets ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">D</span></a> to analyze MAS architecture effect. GPT-4o is used on two comparative cases, one using ChatDev and the other on MetaGPT.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<div id=\"A6.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A6.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">To understand how choices of underlying LLMs and MAS architectures influence failure patterns, we analyze results from our <span id=\"A6.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST-Data</span>, categorized by <span id=\"A6.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> in the Figures <a href=\"#A6.F8\" title=\"Figure 8 ‣ Appendix F Understanding Failures: The Impact of Different LLMs and Agent Architectures ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">8</span></a> and <a href=\"#A6.F9\" title=\"Figure 9 ‣ Appendix F Understanding Failures: The Impact of Different LLMs and Agent Architectures ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">9</span></a>.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A6.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A6.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">First, we examine the impact of different LLMs by comparing GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 Sonnet within the MetaGPT framework on programming tasks Figure <a href=\"#A6.F8\" title=\"Figure 8 ‣ Appendix F Understanding Failures: The Impact of Different LLMs and Agent Architectures ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">8</span></a>. Our findings indicate that GPT-4o exhibits substantially fewer failures in FC1 (System Design Issues, e.g., disobeying task or role specifications) and FC2 (Inter-Agent Misalignment, e.g., issues in coordination or communication) compared to Claude 3.7 Sonnet. This suggests GPT-4o may possess stronger capabilities in instruction following or aspects of ‘social reasoning’ for agentic collaboration within this setup. However, both models show a high number of failures in FC3 (Task Verification), indicating that robust verification remains a significant challenge regardless of the LLM used, though GPT-4o has a marginally lower count here.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A6.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A6.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Next, we investigate the effect of MAS architecture by comparing MetaGPT and ChatDev, both using GPT-4o as the underlying LLM, on the ProgramDev-v2 benchmark in Figure <a href=\"#A6.F9\" title=\"Figure 9 ‣ Appendix F Understanding Failures: The Impact of Different LLMs and Agent Architectures ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">9</span></a>. We observe distinct failure profiles: MetaGPT demonstrates significantly fewer failures in FC1 (System Design Issues) and FC2 (Inter-Agent Misalignment) compared to ChatDev. This could imply that MetaGPT’s architecture or operational flow is more effective at maintaining adherence to specifications and ensuring smoother agent coordination with GPT-4o. Interestingly, despite its stronger performance in FC1 and FC2, MetaGPT exhibits a considerably higher number of FC3 (Task Verification) failures than ChatDev.\nThis may stem from the fact that in MetaGPT, the adherence to task specifications and role specifications ar done mostly through SoPs, demonstrating strong performance in FC1 especially. However ChatDev places a higher importance in verification as it is reflected by the specific testing and reviewing phases in ChatDev’s archiectural design, causing fewer verification issues.\nThese results show that both the choice of LLM and the specific design of the MAS architecture critically shape the landscape of potential failures, and improvements likely require a holistic approach considering both aspects.</p>\n</div>\n<div class=\"ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage\"></div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A7\" class=\"ltx_appendix\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix G </span>Approaches and strategies to improve MASs</h2>\n\n<div id=\"A7.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A7.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In this section, we discuss some approaches to make MASs more robust to failures.\nWe categorize these strategies into two main groups:\n(i) <span id=\"A7.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">tactical approaches</span>,\n(ii) <span id=\"A7.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">structural strategies</span>.\nTactical approaches involve straightforward modifications tailored for specific failure modes, such as improving the prompts, topology of the network of agents, and conversation management.\nIn Section <a href=\"#A8\" title=\"Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">H</span></a>, we experiment with such approaches in two case studies, and demonstrate that the effectiveness of these methods is not consistent.\nThis leads us to consider a second category of strategies that are more comprehensive methods with system-wide impacts:\nstrong verification, enhanced communication protocols, uncertainty quantification, and memory and state management.\nThese strategies require more in-depth study and meticulous implementation, and remain open research topics for future exploration. See Table <a href=\"#A7.T4\" title=\"Table 4 ‣ G.2 Structural Strategies ‣ Appendix G Approaches and strategies to improve MASs ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a> for our proposed mapping between different solution strategies and the failure categories.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"A7.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">G.1 </span>Tactical Approaches</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A7.SS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A7.SS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This category includes strategies related to improving prompts and optimizing agent organization and interactions.\nThe prompts of MAS agents should provide clear description of instructions, and the role of each agent should be clearly specified (see <a href=\"#A12.SS2\" title=\"L.2 Structured prompt with verification section ‣ Appendix L AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">L.2</span></a> as an example) <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib58\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">58</a>, <a href=\"#bib.bib59\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">59</a>]</cite>.\nPrompts can also clarify roles and tasks while encouraging proactive dialogue. Agents can re-engage or retry if inconsistencies arise, as shown in Appendix <a href=\"#A12.SS5\" title=\"L.5 Agent Verifier’s System Prompt ‣ Appendix L AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">L.5</span></a> <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib60\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">60</a>]</cite>.\nAfter completing a complex multi-step task, add a self-verification step to the prompt to retrace the reasoning by restating solutions, checking conditions, and testing for errors <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib61\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">61</a>]</cite>.\nHowever, it may miss flaws, rely on vague conditions, or be impractical <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib36\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">36</a>]</cite>.\nMoreover, clear role specifications can be reinforced by defining conversation patterns and setting termination conditions <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib55\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">55</a>, <a href=\"#bib.bib62\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">62</a>]</cite>.\nA modular approach with simple, well-defined agents, rather than complex, multitasked ones, enhances performance and simplifies debugging <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib63\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">63</a>]</cite>.\nThe group dynamics also enable other interesting possibilities of multi-agent systems: different agents can propose various solutions <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib64\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">64</a>]</cite>, discuss their assumptions, and findings (cross-verifications) <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib65\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">65</a>]</cite>.\nFor instance, in <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib66\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">66</a>]</cite>, a multi-agent strategy simulates the academic peer review process to catch deeper inconsistencies.\nAnother set of tactical approaches for cross verifications consist in multiple LLM calls with majority voting or resampling until verification <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib67\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">67</a>, <a href=\"#bib.bib68\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">68</a>]</cite>.\nHowever, these seemingly straightforward solutions often prove inconsistent, echoing our case studies’ findings. This underscores the need for more robust, structural strategies, as discussed in the following sections.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A7.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">G.2 </span>Structural Strategies</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A7.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A7.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Apart from the tactical approaches we discussed above, there exist a need for more involved solutions that will shape the structure of the MAS at hand.\nWe first observe the critical role of verification processes and verifier agents in multi-agent systems.\nOur annotations reveal that weak or inadequate verification mechanisms were a significant contributor to system failures.\nWhile unit test generation aids verification in software engineering <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib69\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">69</a>]</cite>, creating a universal verification mechanism remains challenging. Even in coding, covering all edge cases is complex, even for experts. Verification varies by domain: coding requires thorough test coverage, QA demands certified data checks <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib70\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">70</a>]</cite>, and reasoning benefits from symbolic validation <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib71\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">71</a>]</cite>. Adapting verification across domains remains an ongoing research challenge.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A7.SS2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A7.SS2.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">A complementary strategy to verification is establishing a standardized communication protocol <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib72\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">72</a>]</cite>.\nLLM-based agents mainly communicate via unstructured text, leading to ambiguities. Clearly defining intentions and parameters enhances alignment and enables formal coherence checks during and after interactions.\n<cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib73\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">73</a>]</cite> introduce Multi-Agent Graph Attention, leveraging a graph attention mechanism to model agent interactions and enhance coordination. Similarly, <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib74\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">74</a>]</cite> propose Attentional Communication, enabling agents to selectively focus on relevant information. Likewise, <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib75\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">75</a>]</cite> develop a learned selective communication protocol to improve cooperation efficiency.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A7.SS2.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A7.SS2.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Another important research direction is fine-tuning MAS agents with reinforcement learning.\nAgents can be trained with role-specific algorithms, rewarding task-aligned actions and penalizing inefficiencies.\nMAPPO <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib76\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">76</a>]</cite> optimizes agents’ adherence to defined roles.\nSimilarly, SHPPO <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib77\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">77</a>]</cite> uses a latent network to learn strategies before applying a heterogeneous decision layer.\nOptima <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib78\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">78</a>]</cite> further enhances communication efficiency and task effectiveness through iterative reinforcement learning.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A7.SS2.p4\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A7.SS2.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">On a different note, incorporating probabilistic confidence measures into agent interactions can significantly enhance decision-making and communication reliability.\nDrawing inspiration from the framework proposed by Horvitz et al. <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib79\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">79</a>]</cite>, agents can be designed to take action only when their confidence exceeds a predefined threshold.\nConversely, when confidence is low, agents can pause to gather additional information.\nFurthermore, the system could benefit from adaptive thresholding, where confidence thresholds are dynamically adjusted.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A7.SS2.p5\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A7.SS2.p5.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Although often seen as a single-agent property, memory and state management are crucial for multi-agent interactions, which can enhance context understanding and reduces ambiguity in communication.\nHowever, most research focuses on single-agent systems. MemGPT <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib3\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">3</a>]</cite> introduces OS-inspired context management for an extended context window, while TapeAgents <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib80\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">80</a>]</cite> use a structured, replayable log (“tape”) to iteratively document and refine agent actions, facilitating dynamic task decomposition and continuous improvement.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"A7.T4\" class=\"ltx_table\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\" style=\"font-size:90%;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_table\">Table 4: </span>Solution Strategies vs. Failure Category in Multi-Agent Systems</figcaption>\n<table id=\"A7.T4.4\" class=\"ltx_tabular
