Including all schemas is wasteful; excluding external tools entirely limits capability. <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> adopts lazy discovery: tools are found on-demand through keyword search, and only discovered tool schemas are included in the context.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><a href=\"#S2.F19\" title=\"In 2.4.7 Token-Efficient External Tool Discovery via MCP ‣ 2.4 Tool System ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">19</span></a> illustrates the three-component interaction. The system integrates MCP for dynamic tool connectivity. Users configure external tool servers (database clients, API services, etc.) via management commands. The system maintains a set of discovered tools, including only schemas for tools explicitly searched for or previously invoked. Initial context contains zero external tool schemas. When the agent calls <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">search_tools</span> (e.g., with query <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">\"database query tools\"</span>), the <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.p2.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SearchToolsHandler</span> builds a vocabulary from all registered MCP tool names and descriptions, extracts keywords (tokens of 3+ characters), and scores each tool against the query using vocabulary matching. Top matches are returned to the LLM with names and descriptions. The <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.p2.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">ToolRegistry</span> then marks matched tools as discovered via <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.p2.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">discover_mcp_tool()</span>, adding their schemas to the discovered set so that the next LLM call includes them. Directly invoking an MCP tool by its qualified name (e.g., <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.p2.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">mcp__github__create_issue</span>) auto-discovers it without requiring a prior search. The <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.p2.1.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">McpToolHandler</span> forwards invocations to the appropriate external server, managing serialization and error handling.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"S2.F19\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><img src=\"2603.05344v3/token_efficient_mcp_discovery.png\" id=\"S2.F19.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:648/310;\" width=\"648\" height=\"310\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 19: </span>Sequence within the Tool layer (<a href=\"#S2.F16\" title=\"In Three separated concerns. ‣ 2.4.1 Registry Architecture and Schema Construction ‣ 2.4 Tool System ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">16</span></a>). The LLM issues a <span id=\"S2.F19.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">search_tools</span> call with a natural-language query. The <span id=\"S2.F19.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SearchToolsHandler</span> builds a keyword vocabulary from all registered MCP tool names and descriptions, scores each tool against the query, and returns top matches. The <span id=\"S2.F19.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">ToolRegistry</span> marks matched tools as discovered, including their schemas in subsequent LLM calls. Only discovered tools incur schema cost, reducing baseline token overhead of MCP integration to near zero.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<section id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\"><span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.Px1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">search_tools</span>: Keyword-scored tool discovery.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Three detail levels control context investment: <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.Px1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">names</span> returns only tool names (minimal tokens), <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.Px1.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">brief</span> adds short descriptions, and <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.Px1.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">full</span> triggers full schema inclusion in subsequent LLM calls. Name matches score 2 points and description matches score 1 point; results rank by total score, surfacing the most relevant tools first. This trades discovery overhead (the agent must search, then invoke) for context savings (only relevant tools are loaded). For workflows using few external tools, the savings are substantial; for workflows using many, the overhead accumulates but remains bounded.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Design evolution.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The initial implementation included all external tool schemas in every call, consuming up to 40% of the context before the first user message. Lazy discovery reduced baseline overhead to nearly zero (<math id=\"S2.SS4.SSS7.Px2.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"&lt;\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>5%), growing only as capabilities are actually used.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">2.4.8 </span>Subagent Delegation, Skills, and Batch Execution</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This section describes three tools that extend the agent’s capabilities beyond single-tool invocations: subagent delegation for complex subtasks, skill loading for on-demand domain expertise, and batch execution for multi-tool efficiency.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Subagent delegation via <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">spawn_subagent</span>.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Launches an isolated subagent with its own ReAct loop and filtered tool registry. Each of the eight subagent types restricts available tools to its domain: Code-Explorer (read-only navigation), Planner (read + write for plans), PR-Reviewer (code review with diff analysis), Security-Reviewer (vulnerability scanning), Web-Clone (website replication), Web-Generator (site creation from specifications), Project-Init (scaffold generation), and Ask-User (UI-only structured surveys). The tool isolation ensures subagents cannot accidentally interfere with each other or exceed their intended scope. <a href=\"#A7\" title=\"Appendix G Subagent Capability Matrix ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Appendix</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">G</span></a> provides the complete capability matrix with per-subagent tool lists.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px1.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px1.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">A key design property is automatic parallelization: when the main agent emits multiple <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px1.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">spawn_subagent</span> calls in the same LLM response, the <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px1.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SubAgentManager</span> executes them concurrently via <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px1.p2.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">asyncio.gather()</span>, with each subagent running in a separate thread with its own iteration budget and tool worker pool. This enables the agent to fan out work naturally (e.g., “investigate the authentication module” and “review the database schema” in parallel) without explicit concurrency management.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px1.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px1.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Additional parameters provide flexibility: model override (haiku for fast, low-cost tasks; sonnet for balanced capability; opus for complex reasoning), background execution (agent continues without waiting for completion), and session resume by agent ID (enabling multi-turn subagent workflows where context is preserved across invocations).</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">On-demand skills via <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">invoke_skill</span>.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Skills are modular knowledge units stored as markdown files with YAML frontmatter, providing domain-specific expertise (git conventions, code review checklists, deployment procedures) that would waste context if loaded unconditionally. The system processes skills in two phases:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Phase 1: Metadata discovery.</span> At startup, the <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SkillLoader</span> scans all skill directories, parsing only the YAML frontmatter to extract names and descriptions. This lightweight index is included in the system prompt, enabling the agent to discover available expertise without loading instructional content. Descriptions follow a “Claude Search Optimization” convention where each begins with “Use when…” to specify trigger conditions (e.g., “Use when writing bash scripts that need to wait for external conditions”), optimizing for agent discoverability.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Phase 2: On-demand loading.</span> When the agent determines a skill is relevant, it invokes <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p3.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">invoke_skill</span> with the skill name. The loader reads the full markdown content, strips the frontmatter, and injects the instructional body into the conversation context. A deduplication cache ensures each skill loads at most once per session, preventing context pollution from redundant invocations.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Skills are discovered from three tiers with strict priority ordering: project-local (<span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p4.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">.opendev/skills/</span>, highest priority) for repository-specific conventions, user-global (˜<span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px2.p4.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/.opendev/skills/</span>) for personal preferences across all projects, and built-in (shipped with the package, lowest priority) for default expertise. When two skills share the same name, the higher-priority source takes precedence, enabling project-specific overrides of default behavior.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px3\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Batch execution via <span id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px3.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">batch_tool</span>.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Enables multiple tool calls in a single agent turn, reducing round-trip overhead. The agent specifies the execution mode: <em id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">parallel</em> (thread pool with max 5 concurrent workers) for independent operations like reading multiple files or running multiple searches, or <em id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px3.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">serial</em> for dependent operations like creating a directory then writing a file into it. The agent specifies the mode because only it knows the dependency relationships from context, as the system cannot reliably infer whether operations are independent. Automatic dependency detection was attempted but proved unreliable; explicit agent-specified mode delegating the decision to the entity with full context knowledge solved this cleanly.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px4\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Design evolution.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The initial design had no batch execution; every tool required a full LLM round-trip, and multiple file reads took multiple turns. Skills were originally loaded at startup, consuming context on expertise never used in the session. Subagents initially ran sequentially, even when tasks were independent. The current architecture addresses all three issues: batch execution eliminates unnecessary round-trips, two-phase skill loading reduces baseline overhead to a compact metadata index, and automatic parallelization of subagent calls exploits task independence without requiring the agent to manage concurrency explicitly.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px4.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS4.SSS8.Px4.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The tools above produce artifacts and side effects; the persistence layer ensures these survive across sessions and provides rollback when the agent makes mistakes.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">2.5 </span>Persistence Layer</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The persistence layer stores conversation histories, configuration, model metadata, and file-operation logs using ordinary files on disk: JSON for structured data, JSONL (one JSON object per line) for append-heavy streams, and plain text where simplicity matters. No external database is required.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">All persistent state lives under two root directories. User-global state (settings, caches, installed plugins) goes to <span id=\"S2.SS5.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">~/.opendev/</span>. Project-scoped state (session transcripts, project-specific settings) goes to a subdirectory derived from the project path: <span id=\"S2.SS5.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">~/.opendev/projects/{encoded-path}/</span>, where the project’s absolute path is encoded by replacing path separators with dashes (e.g., <span id=\"S2.SS5.p2.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/Users/alice/myapp</span> becomes <span id=\"S2.SS5.p2.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">-Users-alice-myapp</span>). This separation ensures that conversations about one repository never appear alongside conversations about another, and that project-specific settings do not leak across unrelated codebases.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">2.5.1 </span>Session Storage</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Each conversation is stored as two files: a <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">.json</span> metadata file and a <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">.jsonl</span> transcript file. The metadata file records the session identifier, creation and last-activity timestamps, working directory, title, and summary, but contains no messages. The transcript file stores the actual messages, one per line, each serialized as a JSON object with role, content, timestamp, tool calls, and token counts. Splitting metadata from messages means that listing all sessions (to show the user a session picker) requires reading only the small metadata files rather than loading potentially large transcript histories.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Writing sessions safely.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Sessions are saved through a write flow designed to prevent data loss even under concurrent access. Before writing, the system acquires an exclusive file lock (<span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">fcntl.flock</span>) on the metadata file with a 10-second timeout to prevent deadlocks. The metadata is then written to a temporary file and atomically renamed into place using <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">os.rename()</span>, which on POSIX systems guarantees that the file is either fully written or untouched, never half-written. The transcript file follows the same locking protocol. After both files are updated, the session index is also updated atomically.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Auto-save.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Rather than requiring explicit save commands, the system auto-saves the conversation every 5 turns (configurable via <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">auto_save_interval</span>). Each auto-save writes both the metadata and the full transcript. Between auto-saves, messages exist only in memory. For multi-channel deployments (such as a web interface), a separate append-only path writes each new message individually to the transcript file under an exclusive lock, providing immediate durability at the cost of one file-system call per message.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px3\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Session index.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Listing sessions by scanning every metadata file in the project directory is slow when many sessions accumulate. A lightweight index file (<span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">sessions-index.json</span>) caches the essential fields (session ID, title, message count, last-modified timestamp) at roughly 200 bytes per entry, enabling instant session listing. The index is updated atomically whenever a session is saved. If the index file is missing, corrupted, or has a permission error, the system rebuilds it automatically by scanning all metadata files in the directory, creating entries for each valid session and deleting empty ones. This self-healing behavior means the index never becomes a single point of failure: even if the file is accidentally deleted or corrupted, the next <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">list_sessions</span> call regenerates it transparently.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px4\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Session titles and resumption.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">When a new session is first saved, it has no meaningful title. A lightweight topic-detection model generates a short title (capped at 50 characters) by examining the last 4 messages. This runs on a background daemon thread so that it never blocks the main conversation loop. When the user starts the agent in a project directory without specifying a session, the system defaults to the most recent session for that project, enabling a “continue where I left off” workflow. Sessions from nested subprojects do not appear in the parent project’s list because each project root produces a distinct encoded path.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px5\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Session cost metadata.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Each session’s metadata file includes a <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">cost_tracking</span> object that records cumulative API usage: total input tokens, total output tokens, total cost in USD (computed from model pricing metadata), and the number of API calls. This metadata is updated after every LLM call and persisted with the session. When the user resumes a session via <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">--continue</span>, the <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">CostTracker</span> service restores its state from this metadata, ensuring that the running cost display reflects the full session history rather than only the current invocation.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px6\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Legacy migration.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px6.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS1.Px6.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Earlier versions stored messages inline in the metadata JSON file rather than in a separate JSONL transcript. When the system encounters a session with inline messages and no JSONL file, it automatically migrates the messages to a new JSONL file, clears the inline messages from the metadata, and saves a backup of the original file. This one-time migration is transparent to the user.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">2.5.2 </span>Operation Log and Undo</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Agents make mistakes: they write to the wrong file, make an edit that breaks something, or delete a file the user did not intend to remove. Rather than requiring users to manually undo these changes with version control commands, <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> tracks every file operation (create, modify, delete) in a log and provides a single-command undo.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Each operation record contains the operation type, file path, timestamp, a unique identifier, and the file’s content before the operation. These records are stored in two places: an in-memory list for fast undo during the current session, and a JSONL file (<span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">operations.jsonl</span>) in the session directory for durability. The JSONL log is best-effort: if writing to it fails (for example, due to a permission issue), the failure is logged but does not interrupt the agent’s work. The in-memory list is the primary data source for undo operations.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">When the user invokes undo, the system pops the most recent operation from the in-memory list and reverses it: created files are deleted, modified files are reverted to their backed-up content, and deleted files are restored from the saved copy. The in-memory history is capped at 50 operations to prevent unbounded memory growth. When the cap is reached, the oldest entries are evicted first. In practice, users rarely need to undo operations older than the last dozen or so, so this bound has not been a limitation.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The undo system works alongside version control rather than replacing it. It handles uncommitted changes without requiring the user to know git, and provides lower friction than typing <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.p4.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">git restore</span> for quick corrections after agent mistakes.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Shadow git snapshots.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The in-memory undo log tracks only file operations performed through the agent’s tools. It cannot capture side effects from shell commands (e.g., <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">npm install</span> modifying <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">package-lock.json</span>) or build processes. For comprehensive per-step undo, the system maintains a <em id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">shadow git repository</em>, a bare repository at <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">~/.opendev/snapshot/&lt;project-id&gt;/</span> that shares no history with the user’s actual repository. At every agent step that modifies files, the snapshot system runs <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">git add . &amp;&amp; git write-tree</span> against the project working directory using the shadow repository’s object store, recording a tree hash in the session metadata. The <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/undo</span> command computes a <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">git diff</span> between the current tree and the snapshot tree, identifies changed files, and restores them via <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.8\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">git checkout &lt;hash&gt; -- &lt;file&gt;</span>. The shadow repository’s <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.9\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">.gitignore</span> is synchronized from the real repository to avoid tracking build artifacts. A scheduled cleanup (<span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.10\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">git gc --prune=7.days</span>) keeps the shadow repository compact. This approach leverages git’s content-addressable storage for perfect file-level restoration without interfering with the user’s version control workflow.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5.SSS3\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">2.5.3 </span>Configuration</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Configuration follows a four-tier hierarchy designed so that users get reasonable behavior out of the box but can customize anything at the right scope:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS3.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<ul id=\"S2.SS5.SSS3.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"S2.I9.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">1.</span> \n<div id=\"S2.I9.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S2.I9.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.I9.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Built-in defaults</span> provide a working configuration without any user setup (default model, temperature, auto-save interval, and so on).</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S2.I9.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.5pt;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">2.</span> \n<div id=\"S2.I9.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S2.I9.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.I9.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Environment variables</span> supply API credentials and CI/CD-specific overrides. API keys are <em id=\"S2.I9.i2.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">only</em> loaded from environment variables, never from configuration files, to prevent accidental exposure in version control. If a key is found in a configuration file, it is automatically stripped during loading.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S2.I9.i3\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.5pt;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">3.</span> \n<div id=\"S2.I9.i3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S2.I9.i3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.I9.i3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">User-global settings</span> (<span id=\"S2.I9.i3.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">~/.opendev/settings.json</span>) store cross-project preferences such as the user’s preferred model, UI settings, and tool auto-approval rules.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S2.I9.i4\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.5pt;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">4.</span> \n<div id=\"S2.I9.i4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S2.I9.i4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.I9.i4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Project-local settings</span> (<span id=\"S2.I9.i4.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">&lt;project&gt;/.opendev/settings.json</span>) store repository-specific overrides, such as a different model for a particular codebase or project-specific coding standards.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS3.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS3.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Each tier overrides the one above it: project settings take precedence over user-global settings, which take precedence over environment variables, which take precedence over built-in defaults. The configuration is loaded once at startup and cached in memory; subsequent reads return the cached value without re-reading files.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS3.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS3.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Context window limits are derived automatically from model capabilities rather than requiring explicit configuration. When the user selects a model, the system looks up its maximum context length from the provider cache (described below) and sets the token budget accordingly. This avoids a common source of misconfiguration where users set a context limit that does not match their model’s actual capacity.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">2.5.4 </span>Provider and Model Cache</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The system needs to know what models are available from each provider, along with their capabilities (context length, vision support, pricing). Rather than hardcoding this information, <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> fetches it from an external catalog API and caches the results locally under <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">~/.opendev/cache/</span>.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The cache uses a stale-while-revalidate strategy with a 24-hour time-to-live. On startup, the system checks when the cache was last refreshed by examining the modification time of a <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">.last_sync</span> marker file. If the cache is less than 24 hours old, it is used as-is. If it is stale or missing, the system fetches fresh data from the API, transforms it into per-provider JSON files (one file per provider, containing model names, context lengths, capabilities, and pricing), and updates the marker. If the network fetch fails, the system falls back to the stale cache if one exists, or proceeds without capability information if no cache is available at all. This ensures that the agent can start even when offline: the cache file from the last successful sync provides enough information to operate normally.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Environment overrides (<span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">OPENDEV_MODELS_DEV_PATH</span> for a local catalog file, <span id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p3.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">OPENDEV_DISABLE_REMOTE_MODELS</span> to skip network entirely) allow the cache to be populated without network access, which is useful in air-gapped environments or for testing with a fixed model set.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS5.SSS4.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The architecture described above embodies numerous design decisions whose rationale is not always self-evident from the component descriptions alone. The next section steps back from per-component detail to examine the cross-cutting design tensions (context pressure, behavioral steering, safety enforcement, LLM imprecision, and resource bounding) that shaped these choices and extracts transferable lessons for builders of similar systems.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S3\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_section\">3 </span>Discussion</h2>\n\n<div id=\"S3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The preceding sections describe the architecture and tool ecosystem of <span id=\"S3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> in detail. Here we step back from per-component descriptions and examine five cross-cutting design tensions that shaped the system. Each subsection synthesizes insights that span multiple components and extracts transferable lessons for builders of similar agentic systems.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S3.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">3.1 </span>Context Pressure as the Central Design Constraint</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Unlike CPU or memory, context is consumed by both the system (prompts, tool schemas, safety preambles) and the agent’s own actions (tool outputs, conversation history). Every capability added to the system prompt and every tool result returned to the agent competes for the same finite budget. In our experience, tool outputs (file contents, command results, search hits) consume 70–80% of the context in a typical session, dwarfing the system prompt and the agent’s own reasoning. This makes context utilization the single most important metric for agent longevity, and it imposes a pervasive tension: richer tool outputs improve per-turn accuracy but shorten the session’s useful life.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.SS1.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\"><span class=\"ltx_inline-block\"><svg id=\"S3.SS1.p2.pic1\" class=\"ltx_picture\" height=\"189.45\" overflow=\"visible\" version=\"1.1\" viewBox=\"0 0 650 189.45\" width=\"650\"><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;\" fill=\"#000000\" stroke=\"#000000\" stroke-width=\"0.4pt\" transform=\"translate(0,189.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)\"><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#BFD0E1;\" fill=\"#BFD0E1\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0 0 L 0 189.45 L 650 189.45 L 650 0 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#F6F9FB;\" fill=\"#F6F9FB\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0.55 0.55 L 0.55 168.17 L 649.45 168.17 L 649.45 0.55 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#EEF2F7;\" fill=\"#EEF2F7\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0.55 168.72 L 0.55 188.89 L 649.45 188.89 L 649.45 168.72 Z\"></path></g><g class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS1.p2.pic1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" operation. A graduated approach (monitoring utilization continuously, pruning stale tool outputs before they become irrelevant, masking old observations, and reserving LLM-based summarization for genuine overflow) dramatically outperforms the naive strategy of compacting everything once a hard limit is reached. The fast pruning pass described in <a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS6\" title=\"2.3.6 Adaptive Context Compaction ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.6</span></a> exemplifies this: by walking backwards through tool results and replacing outputs beyond the agent’s working horizon with a <span id=\"S3.SS1.p2.pic1.2.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">[pruned]</span> marker, it often reclaims enough space to avoid expensive LLM compaction entirely. Design graduated reduction stages rather than a single emergency compaction.</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.SS1.p3\" class=\"ltx_para 15.56 14.1)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:44.93em;--ltx-fo-height:6.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"95.32\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 92.63)\" a size threshold, writing the full content to a scratch file and returning only a short preview plus a file reference keeps the context focused on what the agent is actively using (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS2\" title=\"2.3.2 Tool Result Optimization ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.2</span></a>). The agent sees enough to decide whether the full output matters, and can read it on demand. This transforms a context-consumption problem into a retrieval problem, which is strictly cheaper: retrieval costs one tool call, while context consumption is paid on every subsequent LLM invocation for the rest of the session.</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Prompt structure for caching.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">For providers that support prompt caching, splitting the system prompt into a stable prefix and a dynamic suffix, marking the prefix with a cache control header, yields significant input cost savings over a multi-turn session (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS1.Px2\" title=\"Mode-specific variants and variable substitution. ‣ 2.3.1 Dynamic System Prompt Construction ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.1</span></a>). Since the system prompt is re-sent on every LLM call, caching the stable portion amortizes the cost of the system’s richest instructions.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Dual-memory for thinking contexts.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">When providing conversation context to a thinking model, separating compressed long-range context (an LLM summary of the full history) from detailed short-range context (the last several exchanges verbatim) keeps the thinking budget bounded regardless of conversation length while preserving both strategic goals and operational details (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS3\" title=\"2.3.3 Dual-Memory Architecture for Bounded Thinking ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.3</span></a>). A subtlety: iteratively summarizing a summary accumulates distortion over multiple rounds. Periodically regenerating the summary from the full conversation history, rather than compressing the previous summary, corrects this drift.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2\" call as the calibration anchor is essential for accurate context management. Providers inject invisible content (safety preambles, tool schema serializations, internal formatting) that makes local token counting systematically underestimate actual usage. In our system, the discrepancy was large enough to cause compaction to trigger too late, leading to context overflow errors (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS7\" title=\"2.3.7 Context Retrieval and Assembly Pipeline ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.7</span></a>). Always treat the provider’s reported token count as ground truth; local estimates are useful only as a fallback when no prior API response is available.</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S3.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">3.2 </span>Steering Behavior Over Long Horizons</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">System prompt influence decays as conversations grow. Instructions that reliably govern the agent’s first few turns are routinely violated after 30 or more tool calls, when the instruction is far from the model’s attention window and buried under dozens of tool results. Behavioral guidance is therefore a signal-to-noise engineering problem: how to maintain compliance without drowning the context in repeated directives.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.SS2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\"><span class=\"ltx_inline-block\"><svg id=\"S3.SS2.p2.pic1\" class=\"ltx_picture\" height=\"205.28\" overflow=\"visible\" version=\"1.1\" viewBox=\"0 0 650 205.28\" Crucially, these reminders should use <span id=\"S3.SS2.p2.pic1.2.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">role: user</span> rather than <span id=\"S3.SS2.p2.pic1.2.1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">role: system</span>: in our experiments, user-role reminders consistently produced stronger compliance, likely because the model assigns higher salience to recent user messages than to system context that has been pushed down by intervening turns (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS4\" title=\"2.3.4 Context-Aware System Reminders ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.4</span></a>). However, reminder frequency must be capped per type; a reminder injected on every turn becomes background noise that the model learns to ignore, paradoxically reducing compliance.</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.SS2.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\"><span class=\"ltx_inline-block\"><svg class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS2.p3.pic1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:40.85em;\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS2.p3.pic1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.SS2.p3.pic1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif ltx_font_bold\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#25588C;\">Lesson: Separate thinking from action</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity=\"1.0\" transform=\"matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 15.56 14.1)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:44.93em;--ltx-fo-height:6.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"95.32\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 92.63)\" width=\"621.7\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS2.p3.pic1.2\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:44.93em;\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS2.p3.pic1.2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.SS2.p3.pic1.2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#000000;\">When tools are available, LLMs tend to act quickly rather than think deeply. Providing a separate thinking phase with no tool access produces substantially better reasoning traces, because the model is not pressured by the availability of action (<a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS6\" title=\"2.2.6 Extended ReAct Execution Loop ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.6</span></a>). This separation is more effective than asking the model to “think carefully” in the same call where tools are available. The mechanism matters: it is the absence of tool schemas from the API call, not an instruction to refrain from using them, that changes the model’s behavior.</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Explicit decision trees for tool selection.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Agents default to text search (grep) for nearly every lookup, even when a more precise tool exists. This wastes iterations and floods the context with false positives. Encoding a retrieval-tool decision tree directly into the agent’s prompt (routing symbol names to semantic search, string patterns to text search, structural patterns to AST search, and file-name conventions to glob) reduced unnecessary grep calls and improved first-attempt retrieval accuracy. The key is that the decision criteria must be concrete and anchored to observable features of the query (“if the target is a function or class name, use <span id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">find_symbol</span>”), not abstract (“use the most appropriate tool”).</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Provider-conditional prompt sections.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Different LLM providers have meaningfully different capabilities: extended thinking, function calling conventions, context limits. Rather than cluttering the system prompt with provider-agnostic instructions, registering provider-specific sections that load only when the corresponding provider is active keeps the prompt budget focused (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS1.Px2\" title=\"Mode-specific variants and variable substitution. ‣ 2.3.1 Dynamic System Prompt Construction ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.1</span></a>). Unknown providers receive no section; graceful degradation is better than incorrect guidance.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\"><span class=\"ltx_inline-block\"><svg id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1\" class=\"ltx_picture\" height=\"206.05\" overflow=\"visible\" version=\"1.1\" viewBox=\"0 0 650 206.05\" width=\"650\"><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;\" fill=\"#000000\" stroke=\"#000000\" stroke-width=\"0.4pt\" transform=\"translate(0,206.05) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)\"><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#BFD0E1;\" fill=\"#BFD0E1\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0 0 L 0 206.05 L 650 206.05 L 650 0 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#F6F9FB;\" fill=\"#F6F9FB\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0.55 0.55 L 0.55 184.77 L 649.45 184.77 L 649.45 0.55 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#EEF2F7;\" fill=\"#EEF2F7\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0.55 185.33 L 0.55 205.5 L 649.45 205.5 L 649.45 185.33 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#29629B;--ltx-fill-color:#29629B;--ltx-fg-color:#29629B;\" color=\"#29629B\" fill=\"#29629B\" stroke=\"#29629B\" stroke-width=\"2.5pt\"><path style=\"fill:none\" d=\"M 1.73 206.05 L 1.73 0\"></path></g><g fill-opacity=\"1.0\" transform=\"matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 15.56 191.95)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:40.85em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"12.3\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)\" width=\"565.25\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:40.85em;\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif ltx_font_bold\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#25588C;\">Lesson: Separate agent construction from agent execution</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity=\"1.0\" transform=\"matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 15.56 14.1)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:44.93em;--ltx-fo-height:11.55em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"162.51\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 159.82)\" width=\"621.7\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1.2\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:44.93em;\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1.2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1.2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#000000;\">Long-running agents benefit from a clean separation between scaffolding (pre-runtime assembly) and the harness (runtime orchestration). Scaffolding (constructing the system prompt, building tool schemas, registering subagents) runs once before the first prompt and produces a fully initialized agent. The harness then wraps the reasoning loop with tool dispatch, context management, safety enforcement, and session persistence (<a href=\"#S2.SS2\" title=\"2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2</span></a>). This separation prevents construction-time concerns from tangling with runtime concerns: the harness never checks whether the agent is fully initialized, because eager construction guarantees it always is (<a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS1\" title=\"2.2.1 Agent Scaffolding ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.1</span></a>). The practical benefit is that each concern can evolve independently: adding a new tool requires only a registry change at construction time, while changing the compaction strategy requires only a harness change at runtime.</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S3.SS3\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">3.3 </span>Safety Through Architectural Constraints</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Runtime permission checks are the wrong primary abstraction for agent safety. A model that sees a dangerous tool in its schema can reason about invoking it, argue for why it should be allowed, and probe for edge cases in the permission logic. The more robust approach is to make violations structurally impossible: if write tools are absent from the agent’s schema, the agent cannot attempt writes because it never sees a way to invoke them (<a href=\"#S2.SS2\" title=\"2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2</span></a>). This is the difference between a guard rail and a missing road: the model cannot reason about capabilities it does not know exist.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.SS3.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\"><span class=\"ltx_inline-block\"><svg id=\"S3.SS3.p2.pic1\" class=\"ltx_picture\" height=\"171.61\" overflow=\"visible\" version=\"1.1\" viewBox=\"0 0 650 171.61\" width=\"650\"><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;\" fill=\"#000000\" stroke=\"#000000\" stroke-width=\"0.4pt\" transform=\"translate(0,171.61) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)\"><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#BFD0E1;\" fill=\"#BFD0E1\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0 0 L 0 171.61 L 650 171.61 L 650 0 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#F6F9FB;\" fill=\"#F6F9FB\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0.55 0.55 L 0.55 151.56 L 649.45 151.56 L 649.45 0.55 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#EEF2F7;\" fill=\"#EEF2F7\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0.55 152.12 L 0.55 171.06 L 649.45 171.06 L 649.45 152.12 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#29629B;--ltx-fill-color:#29629B;--ltx-fg-color:#29629B;\" color=\"#29629B\" fill=\"#29629B\" stroke=\"#29629B\" stroke-width=\"2.5pt\"><path style=\"fill:none\" d=\"M 1.73 171.61 L 1.73 0\"></path></g><g fill-opacity=\"1.0\" transform=\"matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 15.56 157.51)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:40.85em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.11em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"11.07\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)\" width=\"565.25\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS3.p2.pic1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:40.85em;\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS3.p2.pic1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.SS3.p2.pic1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif ltx_font_bold\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#25588C;\">Lesson: Make unsafe tools invisible, not blocked</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity=\"1.0\" transform=\"matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 15.56 14.1)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:44.93em;--ltx-fo-height:9.15em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"129.3\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 126.61)\" width=\"621.7\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS3.p2.pic1.2\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:44.93em;\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS3.p2.pic1.2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.SS3.p2.pic1.2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#000000;\">Schema gating (removing tools from the agent’s available set rather than checking permissions at call time) is fundamentally more robust than runtime permission checks. When a tool is absent from the schema, the agent cannot attempt to invoke it, argue for an exception, or probe for bypass conditions. Defense-in-depth with independently designed layers ensures that no single bypass compromises safety: schema gating prevents unauthorized attempts, the approval system intercepts operations requiring human review, file freshness validation prevents overwriting concurrent edits, and shadow git snapshots (<a href=\"#S2.SS5.SSS2\" title=\"2.5.2 Operation Log and Undo ‣ 2.5 Persistence Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.5.2</span></a>) make all filesystem changes reversible. These layers are deliberately independent; a bug in one does not weaken another.</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Approval persistence prevents fatigue.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">When a user marks an approval rule as “always allow,” persisting it to disk so it survives session restarts is critical. Without persistence, users must re-approve the same operations every session, causing approval fatigue that leads to blanket auto-approval, defeating the safety system entirely.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Lifecycle hooks as extensibility.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">External scripts that observe or intercept agent lifecycle events enable custom policies, logging, CI integration, and security enforcement without modifying agent code. The hook interface must be designed early: blocking vs. non-blocking semantics, input mutation support, and merged global/project-level configurations are all necessary for hooks to be useful rather than decorative.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Modal priority during interrupt.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">When the user presses an interrupt key while a modal dialog (approval prompt, user question) is active, the system should cancel the dialog rather than interrupting the agent. Interrupting the agent while a dialog is pending creates orphaned UI state (dangling spinners, stale futures, unresolved promises) that requires manual cleanup.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S3.SS4\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">3.4 </span>Designing for Approximate Outputs</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S3.SS4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.SS4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">LLMs reliably produce approximately-correct outputs. Edit targets drift from actual file content: trailing whitespace, indentation differences, escape sequence variations. Recovery strategies reference tools the agent does not have. Search queries route to suboptimal tools. A system that demands exact correctness from the model will spend most of its time in error-recovery loops. The alternative is to design tools and interfaces that absorb LLM imprecision as a first-class property.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.SS4.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\"><span class=\"ltx_inline-block\"><svg id=\"S3.SS4.p2.pic1\" class=\"ltx_picture\" height=\"155.47\" overflow=\"visible\" version=\"1.1\" viewBox=\"0 0 650 155.47\" width=\"650\"><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;\" fill=\"#000000\" stroke=\"#000000\" stroke-width=\"0.4pt\" transform=\"translate(0,155.47) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)\"><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#BFD0E1;\" fill=\"#BFD0E1\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0 0 L 0 155.47 L 650 155.47 L 650 0 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#F6F9FB;\" fill=\"#F6F9FB\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0.55 0.55 L 0.55 134.19 L 649.45 134.19 L 649.45 0.55 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#EEF2F7;\" fill=\"#EEF2F7\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0.55 134.74 L 0.55 154.92 L 649.45 154.92 L 649.45 134.74 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#29629B;--ltx-fill-color:#29629B;--ltx-fg-color:#29629B;\" color=\"#29629B\" fill=\"#29629B\" stroke=\"#29629B\" stroke-width=\"2.5pt\"><path style=\"fill:none\" d=\"M 1.73 style=\"--ltx-fo-width:40.85em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"12.3\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)\" width=\"565.25\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.pic1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:40.85em;\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.pic1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.pic1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif ltx_font_bold\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#25588C;\">Lesson: Design tools to absorb LLM imprecision</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity=\"1.0\" transform=\"matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 15.56 14.1)\"><foreignObject style=\"--ltx-fo-width:44.93em;--ltx-fo-height:7.89em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;\" height=\"111.93\" overflow=\"visible\" transform=\"matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 109.24)\" width=\"621.7\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.pic1.2\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:44.93em;\">\n<span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.pic1.2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.SS4.p2.pic1.2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#000000;\">The edit operation is the clearest example. A strict exact-match edit tool causes the majority of agent errors in practice, not because the agent’s intent is wrong, but because its reproduction of the target text is slightly off. Building a chain of progressively relaxed matchers, where each returns the <em id=\"S3.SS4.p2.pic1.2.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">actual substring found in the file</em> to preserve original formatting, converts these near-misses into successful edits (<a href=\"#S2.SS4.SSS2\" title=\"2.4.2 File Operations ‣ 2.4 Tool System ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.4.2</span></a>). The chain short-circuits on first match, so exact matches incur zero overhead. The general principle: when the agent’s intent is unambiguous but its literal output is imprecise, the tool should bridge the gap rather than reject the attempt.</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.SS4.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\"><span class=\"ltx_inline-block\"><svg id=\"S3.SS4.p3.pic1\" class=\"ltx_picture\" height=\"172.84\" overflow=\"visible\" version=\"1.1\" viewBox=\"0 0 650 172.84\" width=\"650\"><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;\" fill=\"#000000\" stroke=\"#000000\" stroke-width=\"0.4pt\" transform=\"translate(0,172.84) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)\"><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#BFD0E1;\" fill=\"#BFD0E1\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0 0 L 0 172.84 L 650 172.84 L 650 0 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#F6F9FB;\" fill=\"#F6F9FB\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0.55 0.55 L 0.55 151.56 L 649.45 151.56 L 649.45 0.55 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-fill-color:#EEF2F7;\" fill=\"#EEF2F7\" fill-opacity=\"1.0\"><path style=\"stroke:none\" d=\"M 0.55 152.12 L 0.55 172.29 L 649.45 172.29 L 649.45 152.12 Z\"></path></g><g style=\"--ltx-stroke-color:#29629B;--ltx-fill-color:#29629B;--ltx-fg-color:#29629B;\" color=\"#29629B\" fill=\"#29629B\" stroke=\"#29629B\" stroke-width=\"2.5pt\"><path style=\"fill:none\" d=\"M 1.73
