ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 3: </span>Defense-in-depth safety architecture. Five independent layers intercept dangerous actions at progressively lower levels of abstraction, from model reasoning (Layer 1) to user-defined scripts (Layer 5). Each layer operates independently; failure of any single layer does not compromise the remaining four.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<div id=\"S2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Having established the four-layer overview, we now examine each layer in detail, beginning with the agent core that implements the reasoning loop driving all agent behavior.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">2.2 </span>Agent Core Layer</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The agent layer sits between the UI and the tool execution layers (Figure <a href=\"#S2.F2\" title=\"Figure 2 ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2</span></a>). At its center is a single entry point, <span id=\"S2.SS2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">MainAgent</span>, which receives every user prompt and decides how to process it. Understanding this layer requires two perspectives: how agents are <em id=\"S2.SS2.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">assembled</em> before the first prompt arrives (scaffolding), and how the assembled agent <em id=\"S2.SS2.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">processes</em> user messages at runtime (the harness). In this context, a <em id=\"S2.SS2.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">harness</em> is the runtime orchestration layer that wraps the core reasoning loop and coordinates tool execution, context management, safety enforcement, and session persistence around it <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib102\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">102</a>]</cite>. Where scaffolding is concerned with constructing the agent before the first prompt, the harness is concerned with everything that happens after: dispatching tools, compacting context, enforcing safety invariants, and persisting state across turns. The subsections below present these two phases in order, then detail each supporting component individually.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">2.2.1 </span>Agent Scaffolding</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Before the agent can process user prompts, it must be fully assembled. Every agent in <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> is constructed (system prompt compiled, tool schemas built, subagents registered) before the conversation lifecycle begins (<a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS3\" title=\"2.2.3 Conversation Lifecycle ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.3</span></a>). Understanding this construction pipeline clarifies why the runtime can treat all agents uniformly regardless of their role.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Type foundation: BaseAgent and AgentInterface.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">All agents inherit from <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">BaseAgent</span>, an abstract base class that accepts three constructor arguments (<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">config</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">tool_registry</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">mode_manager</span>) and defines four abstract methods: <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">build_system_prompt()</span> assembles the system prompt string, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">build_tool_schemas()</span> returns OpenAI-format tool schemas, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">call_llm()</span> executes a single LLM call, and <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.8\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">run_sync()</span> runs a full ReAct loop. The critical design choice is <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.9\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">eager construction</em>: <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.10\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">BaseAgent.__init__()</span> calls both <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.11\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">build_system_prompt()</span> and <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.12\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">build_tool_schemas()</span> before the constructor returns. By the time <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.13\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">__init__()</span> completes, the agent is fully ready to serve requests, with no lazy prompt assembly, no first-call latency. A concrete <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.14\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">refresh_tools()</span> method re-invokes both build methods when the tool registry changes (e.g., after MCP server discovery or dynamic skill loading). Downstream code depends not on <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.15\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">BaseAgent</span> directly but on <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.16\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">AgentInterface</span>, a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.17\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">@runtime_checkable</span> Protocol requiring the same surface (<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.18\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">system_prompt</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.19\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">tool_schemas</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.20\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">refresh_tools</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.21\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">call_llm</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.22\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">run_sync</span>), which decouples the factory from the concrete agent class.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Single concrete agent class.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">There is no class hierarchy of agent types. <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">MainAgent</span> is the only concrete subclass of <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">BaseAgent</span>, and every agent in the system (the main agent, all builtin subagents, and any user-defined custom agents) is an instance of this single class. Behavioral variation comes entirely from construction parameters: <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">allowed_tools</span> (a list that filters which tool schemas appear in the agent’s schema, or <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">None</span> for full access), <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">_subagent_system_prompt</span> (an override prompt set after construction), and an <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">is_subagent</span> flag derived from whether <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">allowed_tools</span> is non-null. Within <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.8\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">__init__</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.9\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">MainAgent</span> sets four HTTP client slots to <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.10\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">None</span> for lazy initialization, one each for the normal, thinking, critique, and VLM providers, deferring API key validation until the first LLM call. It creates a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.11\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">ToolSchemaBuilder(registry, allowed_tools)</span> for schema generation and a bounded <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.12\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">Queue(maxsize=10)</span> for thread-safe message injection from the Web UI. The lazy client slots correspond to the model roles described in <a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS5\" title=\"2.2.5 Workload-Optimized Multi-Model Architecture ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.5</span></a>: each slot materializes a provider-specific HTTP client on first access, allowing agents to be constructed before credentials are configured.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Factory assembly.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">AgentFactory</span> is the single entry point for agent construction. Both the TUI and Web UI invoke the same <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">create_agents()</span> method, ensuring identical setup regardless of frontend. The factory executes three phases in strict order:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Phase 1 (Skills).</em> The factory discovers skill definitions from three directories (builtin, user global, and project-local), creates a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SkillLoader</span>, and registers it with the tool registry so that the <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p2.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">use_skill</span> tool becomes available.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Phase 2 (Subagents).</em> The factory creates a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p3.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SubAgentManager</span>, calls <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p3.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">register_defaults()</span> to compile the builtin subagent specifications, then calls <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p3.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">_register_custom_agents()</span> to load any user-defined agents from configuration files. Finally, it registers the manager with the tool registry via <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p3.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">set_subagent_manager()</span>, which makes the <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p3.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">spawn_subagent</span> tool available.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p4.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Phase 3 (Main agent).</em> The factory constructs a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p4.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">MainAgent</span> with no tool filtering (full access to all registered tools, including those added in Phases 1 and 2).</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p5\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p5.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The ordering constraint is essential: Phase 2 must complete before Phase 3 because the <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p5.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">spawn_subagent</span> tool description is dynamically built from the set of registered agents, and it must be present in the main agent’s schema. The factory returns an <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p5.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">AgentSuite</span> dataclass bundling the main agent, the <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p5.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SubAgentManager</span>, and the <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p5.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SkillLoader</span>.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Subagent compilation.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Each subagent begins as a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SubAgentSpec</span>, a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">TypedDict</span> containing a name, description, system prompt, optional tool allowlist, optional model override, and optional Docker configuration. When <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SubAgentManager.register_subagent(spec)</span> is called, it executes a four-step pipeline: (1) resolve the tool list, defaulting to a hardcoded set of safe tools if none is specified; (2) create an <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">AppConfig</span> copy with the model override if one is provided; (3) construct a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">MainAgent</span> with <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">allowed_tools</span> set to the resolved list, triggering the eager build of a filtered system prompt and tool schema; and (4) set <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">agent._subagent_system_prompt</span> to the spec’s prompt override. The result is stored as a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.8\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">CompiledSubAgent</span> (name, description, agent instance, tool list). Construction is cheap because all subagents share the same tool registry reference, with no cloning or deep copying. Runtime isolation comes from two mechanisms: schema filtering at build time (the subagent never sees tools outside its allowlist) and <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.9\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">message_history=None</span> at execution time (each invocation starts with a fresh context, as detailed in <a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS7\" title=\"2.2.7 Subagent Orchestration ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.7</span></a>).</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Dependency injection.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Agent construction produces agents; runtime execution requires <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">services</em>. <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">AgentDependencies</span> is a Pydantic model carrying seven fields that tools need at execution time: <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">mode_manager</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">approval_manager</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">undo_manager</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">session_manager</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">working_dir</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.8\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">console</span>, and <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.9\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">config</span>. The REPL or Web UI constructs this object with all managers and passes it to <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.10\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">agent.run_sync()</span>. Inside the ReAct loop (<a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS6\" title=\"2.2.6 Extended ReAct Execution Loop ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.6</span></a>), individual managers are unpacked from the dependencies object and passed as keyword arguments to <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.11\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">execute_tool()</span>, keeping the tool registry interface flat: it does not depend on the <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.12\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">AgentDependencies</span> model directly. Subagents receive a lightweight <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.13\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SubAgentDeps</span> dataclass with only three fields: <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.14\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">mode_manager</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.15\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">approval_manager</span>, and <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.16\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">undo_manager</span>. The omitted fields enforce an isolation boundary: subagents do not get <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.17\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">session_manager</span> (their messages are not persisted), <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.18\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">console</span> (output flows through <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.19\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">ui_callback</span>), or <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.20\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">config</span> (each subagent carries its own configuration from construction).</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px6\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Design evolution.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px6.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px6.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Three design pivots shaped the current scaffolding architecture. First, an early class hierarchy, with separate classes for planning agents, code-exploration agents, and web-generation agents, was replaced by the single parameterized <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px6.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">MainAgent</span>. The hierarchy created a diamond problem when subagents needed mixed capabilities (e.g., a web generator that also plans), and the parameterized approach eliminated it entirely. Second, lazy prompt building (constructing the system prompt on the first <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px6.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">run_sync</span> call) was replaced by the eager-build pattern. The lazy approach introduced first-call latency visible to the user and caused race conditions with MCP server discovery: tools registered after the first call would not appear in the prompt until a manual refresh. Eager building guarantees that every agent is complete at construction time. Third, inline subagent definitions, where hardcoded agent construction within the main agent’s code, were replaced by the <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS1.Px6.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SubAgentSpec</span> registration system. This refactoring enabled custom agents defined in configuration files to go through the same compilation path as builtin agents, unifying the two code paths.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">2.2.2 </span>Agent Runtime Architecture</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">With scaffolding complete, the assembled agent is ready to process user messages. The runtime behavior is governed by the agent harness, the orchestration infrastructure introduced in <a href=\"#S2.SS2\" title=\"2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2</span></a> that turns a stateless LLM into a persistent, tool-using, self-correcting agent. <a href=\"#S2.F4\" title=\"In 2.2.2 Agent Runtime Architecture ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a> maps this harness architecture: the ReAct execution loop at the center, surrounded by the subsystems that feed it, constrain it, and persist its work.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"S2.F4\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><img src=\"2603.05344v3/agent_harness.png\" id=\"S2.F4.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:648/329;\" width=\"648\" height=\"329\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 4: </span>The agent harness architecture: a detailed view of the Agent layer from <a href=\"#S2.F2\" title=\"In 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2</span></a>. The central ReAct loop (six phases: pre-check and compaction, thinking, self-critique, action, tool execution, post-processing) is surrounded by seven supporting subsystems. User messages enter through a message injection queue (top). The Prompt Composition engine assembles modular sections by priority into the system prompt. The Tool Registry dispatches to specialized handlers, with MCP tools discovered lazily. The Safety System enforces multiple independent layers (approval, dangerous command detection, hooks, stale-read detection, plan mode restrictions, doom loop detection, iteration cap, cooperative cancellation). Context Engineering applies five-stage progressive compaction as the conversation grows. Memory and Session services provide persistent strategy memory (playbook), session storage, and per-step undo via git snapshots. Subagent Orchestration spawns isolated agent instances with filtered tool access for parallel exploration or specialized tasks.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">The central execution cycle.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The ReAct loop at the center of <a href=\"#S2.F4\" title=\"In 2.2.2 Agent Runtime Architecture ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a> executes six phases per iteration: pre-check and compaction, thinking, self-critique, action, tool execution, and post-processing. Each phase is a distinct stage in the executor pipeline: pre-check drains injected messages and compacts under memory pressure, thinking and self-critique produce optional chain-of-thought traces, the action phase calls the LLM with full tool schemas, tool execution dispatches calls through the registry with approval checks, and post-processing decides whether to iterate or return. The cycle repeats until the agent produces a final text response with no tool calls, or until a safety cap is reached. <a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS6\" title=\"2.2.6 Extended ReAct Execution Loop ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.6</span></a> details the per-phase algorithms and control flow.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Input and output boundaries.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">At the top of <a href=\"#S2.F4\" title=\"In 2.2.2 Agent Runtime Architecture ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a>, the Input Layer accepts user messages through a thread-safe bounded queue, allowing follow-up messages to arrive while the agent is mid-execution. Configuration and settings flow in alongside the message queue, providing the agent with its runtime parameters (model selection, approval level, working directory). At the bottom, the Post-Processing path handles three responsibilities after the loop terminates: persisting the updated conversation to the session store, executing any registered Stop hooks, and returning the agent’s final response to the UI layer for rendering.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px3\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Supporting subsystems.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The periphery of <a href=\"#S2.F4\" title=\"In 2.2.2 Agent Runtime Architecture ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a> shows seven subsystems, each addressing a distinct concern and detailed in a dedicated section. The Prompt Composition engine (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS1.Px2\" title=\"Mode-specific variants and variable substitution. ‣ 2.3.1 Dynamic System Prompt Construction ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.1</span></a>) assembles the system prompt from modular sections (identity, safety policy, tool guidance, workflow rules, and dynamic context), split into cacheable and non-cacheable segments for efficient API caching. The Tool Registry (<a href=\"#S2.SS4.SSS1\" title=\"2.4.1 Registry Architecture and Schema Construction ‣ 2.4 Tool System ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.4.1</span></a>) dispatches each tool call to specialized handlers, with MCP tools discovered lazily at runtime. The Safety System (<a href=\"#S2.SS1.SSS0.Px5\" title=\"Safety Architecture. ‣ 2.1 Overview ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.1</span></a>) provides defense in depth through multiple independent layers, where no single layer is relied upon exclusively and each catches a different failure mode. Context Engineering (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS6\" title=\"2.3.6 Adaptive Context Compaction ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.6</span></a>) manages the conversation as a finite resource, applying progressively aggressive compaction as token usage grows. Memory and Session services (<a href=\"#S2.SS5\" title=\"2.5 Persistence Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.5</span></a>) persist both the conversation transcript and a playbook of learned strategies that evolve based on feedback. Subagent Orchestration (<a href=\"#S2.SS2.SSS7\" title=\"2.2.7 Subagent Orchestration ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.2.7</span></a>) enables the main agent to delegate specialized tasks (code exploration, security review, web generation) to isolated agent instances that share the same tool infrastructure but operate with filtered tool access and independent conversation histories.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px3.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px3.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The key architectural decision is that the system operates in two distinct modes, <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px3.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Plan Mode</em> and <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px3.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Normal Mode</em>, with the agent transitioning between them based on user commands or prompt triggers. <a href=\"#S2.F5\" title=\"In Supporting subsystems. ‣ 2.2.2 Agent Runtime Architecture ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">5</span></a> illustrates this dual-mode flow.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"S2.F5\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><img src=\"2603.05344v3/normal_and_plan_mode.png\" id=\"S2.F5.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:648/378;\" width=\"648\" height=\"378\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 5: </span>Dual-mode operation within the Agent layer (<a href=\"#S2.F4\" title=\"In 2.2.2 Agent Runtime Architecture ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a>). A user prompt enters the <span id=\"S2.F5.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">MainAgent</span>, which routes to either Plan Mode (left, read-only) or Normal Mode (right, full access). Plan Mode spawns a Planner subagent that explores the codebase, analyzes patterns, and produces a structured plan for user approval. Upon approval, the system transitions to Normal Mode, where the agent executes the planned steps with full tool access. The user can re-enter Plan Mode at any point if unexpected results require re-planning.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px4\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Routing: plan or execute.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">When a user prompt arrives, the <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">MainAgent</span> checks whether it should enter Plan Mode or proceed directly in Normal Mode. Two triggers activate Plan Mode: an explicit <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px4.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/plan</span> command from the user, or a heuristic that detects planning intent in the prompt (e.g., requests to “design,” “architect,” or “plan” a change). All other prompts proceed in Normal Mode by default. This routing is a one-time decision per prompt; the agent does not switch modes mid-execution unless the user explicitly requests it.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Plan Mode: subagent-based planning.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Rather than switching the main agent into a restricted mode via dedicated plan-management tools, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> delegates planning to a first-class <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">Planner</span> subagent. When planning is needed, the main agent calls <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">spawn_subagent(type=\"Planner\")</span>, which launches a subagent with read-only tools and a specialized planning prompt. Write operations are excluded from the subagent’s tool schema entirely: the LLM never sees tool definitions it cannot use, eliminating the possibility of write attempts during planning.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The Planner subagent executes in three stages visible in <a href=\"#S2.F5\" title=\"In Supporting subsystems. ‣ 2.2.2 Agent Runtime Architecture ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">5</span></a>. First, it <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">explores</em> the codebase using read-only tools: reading files, searching code, listing directory contents, and resolving symbol definitions. Second, it <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">analyzes</em> the findings, identifying patterns, evaluating risks, considering trade-offs, and determining the sequence of changes needed. Third, it <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p2.1.3\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">writes a structured plan</em> to a file in the scratch directory, containing seven sections: goal, context, files to modify, new files to create, implementation steps, verification criteria, and risks.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Upon completion, the Planner returns the plan file path to the main agent. The main agent then calls <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">present_plan(plan_file_path)</span>, which displays the plan to the user for review. The user has two choices: <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p3.1.2\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">revise</em> (the main agent can spawn the Planner again with feedback) or <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p3.1.3\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">approve</em> (the agent proceeds to execution in Normal Mode). This design eliminates the need for a separate mode manager state: the main agent stays in Normal Mode throughout, and planning is simply a subagent delegation.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px6\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Normal Mode: full execution.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px6.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px6.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Normal Mode is the default and only operating state. The agent has full access to all tools, including file reading, file writing, code editing, command execution, and subagent spawning. After a plan is approved via <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px6.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">present_plan</span>, the agent works through the planned steps, using the task management tools to track progress.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px6.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px6.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">During execution, if the agent encounters unexpected results (such as a test failure that reveals a deeper issue, a dependency conflict, or a scope change), it can spawn the Planner subagent again with the current codebase state as context, producing a revised plan that accounts for what has changed since the original plan was approved.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px7\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Rationale for subagent-based planning.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px7.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px7.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The initial design used a four-tool state machine (<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px7.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">enter_plan_mode</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px7.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">exit_plan_mode</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px7.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">create_plan</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px7.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">edit_plan</span>) that switched the main agent into a restricted planning state. This was brittle: the agent sometimes failed to exit plan mode, leaving the system stuck in a read-only state requiring manual intervention.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px7.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px7.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The current design eliminates this state machine entirely. Planning is delegated to a Planner subagent with a schema that contains only read-only tools, enforcing the separation at the schema level rather than through runtime permission checks. The Planner cannot write because write tools do not exist in its schema, not because a runtime check blocks the attempt. This yields three advantages: (1) no state machine means no risk of getting stuck in plan mode; (2) the Planner can be spawned concurrently with other subagents (e.g., a Code Explorer for parallel analysis); and (3) the tool surface is reduced from four tools to one (<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS2.Px7.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">present_plan</span>), reducing cognitive load on the LLM.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">2.2.3 </span>Conversation Lifecycle</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><a href=\"#S2.F6\" title=\"In 2.2.3 Conversation Lifecycle ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">6</span></a> traces the end-to-end path of a single user message through the system, from initial input to final session persistence.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"S2.F6\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><img src=\"2603.05344v3/conversation_lifecycle.png\" id=\"S2.F6.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:648/344;\" width=\"648\" height=\"344\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 6: </span>Sequence diagram of a single conversation turn in <span id=\"S2.F6.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span>. A user message enters through one of three interfaces, passes through query processing, and enters the ReAct iteration loop. Each iteration comprises context management, optional thinking, an action LLM call, and tool dispatch through the registry. The loop continues until the agent signals completion or a termination condition is met, after which the conversation state is persisted.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Input ingestion and query processing.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">User input arrives through one of three entry paths: a non-interactive CLI invocation that creates a one-shot session, the TUI that wraps an interactive REPL, or the Web UI that accepts messages over WebSocket. All three paths converge on the same agent execution core. The TUI path applies a pre-processing stage before entering the ReAct loop: persisting the message to the session store, firing lifecycle hooks that can inspect or modify the query, expanding inline file references (e.g., <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">@file</span>) into their contents, and assembling the message list in the format expected by the LLM API. The Web and CLI paths invoke the agent directly without pre-processing.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">The iteration cycle.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Each iteration of the ReAct loop follows a fixed sequence. First, the executor drains any messages that the UI thread injected since the last iteration, such as follow-up instructions or system signals delivered through a thread-safe queue. Second, the context compactor checks token utilization against the context window and applies reduction strategies if pressure is rising (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS6\" title=\"2.3.6 Adaptive Context Compaction ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.6</span></a> describes the compaction mechanism). Third, if thinking mode is enabled, a separate LLM call produces a reasoning trace without tool access, preventing premature action. Fourth, the action model receives the full conversation, including any thinking trace, along with the available tool schemas, and returns a response that may contain text, tool calls, or both. When tool calls are present, the executor dispatches them through the tool registry: read-only tools run in parallel via a thread pool (up to five concurrent calls), while write tools run sequentially. If a tool call delegates to a subagent, that subagent runs in an isolated context with filtered tool access and returns a summary to the parent agent.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px3\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Completion and persistence.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The loop terminates through one of four paths: the agent responds with text and no tool calls (implicit completion), the agent explicitly signals done via a completion tool, the error-recovery budget is exhausted (the system injects up to three targeted recovery messages per error sequence (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS5\" title=\"2.3.5 Context-Injected Error Recovery ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.5</span></a>)), or the iteration count reaches the safety limit. Before accepting termination, the system checks for incomplete task items and pending messages in the injection queue (a thread-safe channel through which the UI can deliver messages mid-execution), deferring completion if either condition holds. Once accepted, the final conversation state is saved to the session store.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Lifecycle hooks.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> exposes lifecycle events that external scripts can observe or intercept: <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SessionStart</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">UserPromptSubmit</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">PreToolUse</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">PostToolUse</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">PostToolUseFailure</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SubagentStart</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.8\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SubagentStop</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.9\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">Stop</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.10\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">PreCompact</span>, and <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.11\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SessionEnd</span>. Hook commands are configured via JSON in global or project settings and receive event context on stdin as JSON. Blocking events (<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.12\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">PreToolUse</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.13\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">UserPromptSubmit</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.14\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">SubagentStart</span>) can prevent the operation (exit code 2 returns a block reason to the agent), mutate tool arguments (stdout JSON with <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px4.p1.1.15\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">tool_input</span> key), or override approval decisions. Non-blocking events fire asynchronously after the operation completes. Global and project hooks merge by appending project matchers after global matchers per event type, enabling organization-wide policies combined with repository-specific hooks (e.g., “run eslint after file edits”).</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Cross-cutting concerns.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Three mechanisms operate across all phases of the lifecycle.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Interrupt tokens</em> propagate cancellation requests from the UI to the agent thread, polled at six phase boundaries within each iteration (before and after thinking, before action, during tool execution, and at iteration boundaries). The interrupt system addresses several race conditions through targeted fixes: modal controllers (ask-user dialogs, plan approval) take priority over agent interrupts to prevent orphaned UI state; subprocess creation uses process groups (<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">start_new_session=True</span>) so that <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p2.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">os.killpg</span> reliably terminates child processes; and a one-shot guard prevents duplicate interrupt messages from rapid key presses.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">A <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">thread-safe injection queue</em> allows users to send follow-up messages while the agent is mid-execution; these messages are drained at iteration boundaries and checked before completion, ensuring that no user input is silently dropped.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p4.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Session cost tracking</em> records cumulative token usage and cost after each LLM call via a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p4.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">CostTracker</span> service that computes cost from the API’s reported token counts and the model’s pricing metadata; running totals are displayed in the TUI status bar and persisted in session metadata for resumption across <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS3.Px5.p4.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">--continue</span> invocations.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">2.2.4 </span>REPL Command Dispatch</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The conversation lifecycle described above assumes that user input enters the agent reasoning loop. However, not all input requires LLM involvement. Session management, mode switching, model selection, and MCP server configuration are deterministic operations that can be handled directly by the REPL without invoking the agent. The system therefore implements a dual-path dispatch at the input boundary: if the input begins with a “<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/</span>” prefix, it is routed to a registered command handler; otherwise, it proceeds to the query processor and enters the agent loop. <a href=\"#S2.F7\" title=\"In 2.2.4 REPL Command Dispatch ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">7</span></a> illustrates this architecture.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"S2.F7\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><img src=\"2603.05344v3/repl_system.png\" id=\"S2.F7.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:648/264;\" width=\"648\" height=\"264\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 7: </span>Dual-path input dispatch in <span id=\"S2.F7.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span>. User input is classified at the REPL boundary: slash commands (top path) are routed through the REPL Command Dispatcher to one of nine registered command handlers, each of which modifies system state directly and returns a <span id=\"S2.F7.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">CommandResult</span>. Natural language queries (bottom path) pass through the Query Processor into the Agent Loop, which interacts with system state through tool execution. Both paths ultimately produce side effects on shared system state, but through fundamentally different mechanisms: commands execute deterministically without LLM involvement, while queries are processed through the full reasoning loop.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Command handler abstraction.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">All command handlers extend a common abstract base class that provides the handler interface and standardized output formatting. Each handler receives a reference to the REPL instance at construction, granting access to the shared managers (session, mode, configuration, MCP) through explicit dependency injection rather than global state. The handler’s <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">handle(args)</span> method performs argument parsing, executes the operation, and returns a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px1.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">CommandResult</span> containing a success flag, a human-readable message, and optional structured data. Commands with subcommands (e.g., <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px1.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/mcp connect</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px1.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/agents create</span>) perform a second-level split on the argument string and dispatch internally to the appropriate method.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Handler categories.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">As shown in <a href=\"#S2.F7\" title=\"In 2.2.4 REPL Command Dispatch ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">7</span></a>, nine handler classes cover the system’s interactive control surface. <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Session commands</em> (<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/clear</span>, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/compact</span>) manage conversation state: clearing saves the current session and starts fresh, while compacting triggers context reduction on demand. <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Mode commands</em> (<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/mode</span>) switch between normal and plan mode by setting a pending flag that the query processor reads on the next user query. <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.6\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Configuration commands</em> (<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/models</span>) present an interactive model selector that, upon selection, triggers a full agent rebuild with the new model configuration. <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.8\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">MCP commands</em> (<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.9\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/mcp</span>) expose eleven subcommands for managing Model Context Protocol servers: connecting, disconnecting, listing tools, and testing server health. <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.10\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Agent</em>, <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.11\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">skills</em>, and <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.12\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">plugin commands</em> manage custom agent definitions, reusable prompt templates, and third-party extensions, respectively. <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.13\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Tool commands</em> (<span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.14\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/init</span>) initialize codebase context, and a <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px2.p1.1.15\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">help command</em> lists all available commands.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px3\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Side effects on system state.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Commands do not produce isolated outputs; they modify shared state that subsequent agent interactions depend on. As depicted in the right column of <a href=\"#S2.F7\" title=\"In 2.2.4 REPL Command Dispatch ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">7</span></a>, both command handlers and the agent loop converge on the same system state. For example, <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/models</span> triggers a full reconstruction of the agent factory, rebuilding tool registries and system prompts with the new model’s capabilities. <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px3.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/mcp connect</span> discovers and registers new tools from the connected server, expanding the tool schemas available to the agent on its next turn. <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px3.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">/mode plan</span> sets a flag that causes the query processor to activate planning behavior on the next query. These side effects are the primary mechanism through which commands influence agent behavior without directly entering the reasoning loop.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px4\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Separation from agent tools.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS4.Px4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The distinction between REPL commands and agent tools is architectural, not incidental. Commands are triggered by the user typing a slash prefix, executed synchronously by the REPL, and require no LLM involvement, no tool-use hooks, no approval gates, and no undo tracking. Agent tools, by contrast, are selected by the LLM during reasoning, executed through the tool registry with pre- and post-execution hooks, subject to user approval based on the configured autonomy level, and tracked by the undo manager. Commands operate on the REPL instance; tools operate within a run context that carries agent dependencies. This separation ensures that system-level operations (changing models, managing servers, resetting sessions) remain fast and predictable, while delegating open-ended problem-solving to the agent loop.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS5\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">2.2.5 </span>Workload-Optimized Multi-Model Architecture</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">A core realization of the compound AI systems paradigm <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib103\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">103</a>]</cite> is that different execution phases benefit from different model capabilities. Reasoning tasks benefit from extended thinking without tool distraction. Visual tasks require vision-language models. Bulk summarization benefits from cheaper, faster models. Using a single model for all tasks either wastes cost (using expensive models for simple tasks) or sacrifices quality (using cheap models for complex reasoning). Three approaches were considered: a single model for everything (simple but inflexible), task-specific routing (adopted here, which introduces complexity in selection logic but enables workload optimization), and ensemble execution (maximum quality but prohibitive latency and cost).</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS5.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Five model roles with fallback chains.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS5.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS5.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Five distinct workload categories route to specialized models:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS5.Px1.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<ul id=\"S2.SS2.SSS5.Px1.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"S2.I1.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S2.I1.i1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S2.I1.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.I1.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Action model:</span> Primary execution model for tool-based reasoning. Default for all workloads unless a specialized model is specified.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S2.I1.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S2.I1.i2.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S2.I1.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.I1.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Thinking model:</span> Optional model for extended reasoning without tool access. Enables focus on strategic planning without tool-calling pressure. Fallback: action model.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S2.I1.i3\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S2.I1.i3.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S2.I1.i3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.I1.i3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.I1.i3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Critique model:</span> Optional model for self-evaluation. Inspired by Reflexion <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib74\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">74</a>]</cite> but applied selectively rather than on every turn. Fallback: thinking model <math id=\"S2.I1.i3.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\to\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo stretchy=\"false\">→</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\to</annotation></semantics></math> action model.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S2.I1.i4\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S2.I1.i4.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S2.I1.i4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.I1.i4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.I1.i4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Vision model:</span> Vision-language model for processing screenshots and images. Essential for visual debugging tasks. Fallback: action model if vision-capable.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S2.I1.i5\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\"><math id=\"S2.I1.i5.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\bullet\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> \n<div id=\"S2.I1.i5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S2.I1.i5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.I1.i5.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Compact model:</span> Smaller, faster model for summarization during context compaction. Prioritizes speed and cost over reasoning depth. Fallback: action model.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS5.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Provider abstraction and caching.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS5.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS5.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Each model selection triggers lazy initialization of provider-specific API clients, reducing startup latency, as only models actually used in a session are initialized. Model capabilities (context length, vision support, reasoning features) are cached locally with time-to-live refresh, enabling offline startup and background updates following a stale-while-revalidate pattern. The cache trades potential staleness for startup reliability, with background refresh ensuring eventual consistency.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">2.2.6 </span>Extended ReAct Execution Loop</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Once a mode is selected, the agent processes each user query through the <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">ReactExecutor</span>, which implements an extended version of the Reason-Act loop <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib99\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">99</a>]</cite> (referred to simply as the <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">ReAct loop</em> throughout this paper). <a href=\"#S2.F8\" title=\"In 2.2.6 Extended ReAct Execution Loop ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">8</span></a> illustrates the full execution pipeline.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"S2.F8\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><img src=\"2603.05344v3/react_executor_loop_architecture.png\" id=\"S2.F8.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:648/336;\" width=\"648\" height=\"336\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 8: </span>Detailed view of the ReAct loop at the center of <a href=\"#S2.F4\" title=\"In 2.2.2 Agent Runtime Architecture ‣ 2.2 Agent Core Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Figure</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a>. Each user query passes through an initialization stage that creates an <span id=\"S2.F8.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">IterationContext</span>, then enters an iteration loop (<span id=\"S2.F8.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">_run_iteration_inner</span>) consisting of four phases: context management, thinking, action, and decision. The loop continues until the agent produces a final response, explicitly signals completion, or exhausts its iteration budget.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Standard ReAct <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib99\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">99</a>]</cite> interleaves reasoning and action in the same turn, which limits deliberation. Tool schemas consume context and create pressure to act quickly rather than think deeply. Four approaches were considered: pure ReAct (simple but biased toward premature action), chain-of-thought prompting (inflexible because it cannot adapt depth to task complexity), a separate thinking phase (enables depth control and prevents premature tool use), and Reflexion-inspired self-critique loops (maximum quality but doubles thinking latency). <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps\">OpenDev</span> combines the latter two: an explicit thinking phase before action, with optional self-critique for complex tasks.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"alg1\" latency\n\n</div>\n</div>\n</figure>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px1\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Initialization.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">When a query arrives, the executor clears any pending injection queue, creates an interrupt token for cancellation support, wraps the conversation history in a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">ValidatedMessageList</span> (which enforces correct message alternation), and bundles everything into an <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px1.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">IterationContext</span>. This context object carries all per-query state: iteration counters, one-shot guard flags (to prevent duplicate signals), and references to shared services such as the tool registry and approval manager.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px2\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Phase 0: Staged context management.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">At the start of each iteration, the executor drains the injection queue and runs the <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">staged compactor</em>. The compactor monitors token utilization against the context window and applies five progressively aggressive reduction strategies as pressure rises: warning (70%), observation masking (80%), fast pruning (85%), aggressive masking (90%), and full LLM-based compaction (99%). <a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS6\" title=\"2.3.6 Adaptive Context Compaction ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.6</span></a> details each stage; the key property is that cheaper strategies (masking, pruning) often reclaim sufficient space, avoiding the cost of full LLM summarization.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px3\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Phase 1: Thinking.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">If thinking mode is enabled, the executor calls a separate thinking LLM with a tool-free copy of the conversation. This model produces a reasoning trace (a structured analysis of the current situation, potential approaches, and risks) without access to tools, so it cannot take premature action. Separating thinking from action prevents premature tool use: when tools are available, models tend to act quickly rather than think deeply. Four configurable depth levels (OFF, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH) let users balance latency against deliberation quality on a per-task basis. At the HIGH level, self-critique is automatically included: a critique model evaluates the initial trace, and the thinking model refines its reasoning with the critique as additional input. An earlier design exposed self-critique as a separate fifth level, but users found the distinction confusing; merging it into HIGH simplified the interface without reducing capability, since users who want deep thinking invariably benefit from critique as well. The final trace is injected into the conversation as a system reminder, making the reasoning visible to the action model in the next phase.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px4\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Phase 2: Action.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The executor assembles the full action prompt: the system prompt (composed by <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">PromptComposer</span> from priority-ordered sections), selected memory bullets from the ACE playbook (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS6\" title=\"2.3.6 Adaptive Context Compaction ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.6</span></a>), all tool schemas, and the conversation history including any injected thinking trace. This prompt is sent to the action LLM, which returns a response that may contain text, tool calls, or both. The API’s reported token count is used to calibrate the compactor’s utilization estimates for Phase 0 of the next iteration.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Phase 3: Decision, dispatch, and doom-loop detection.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The executor branches based on whether the action model produced tool calls. If no tool calls are present: when the previous tool failed, the executor classifies the error (permission denied, file not found, syntax error, rate limit, etc.) and injects a targeted recovery nudge (<a href=\"#S2.SS3.SSS5\" title=\"2.3.5 Context-Injected Error Recovery ‣ 2.3 Context Engineering Layer ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal:Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">Section</span> <span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.3.5</span></a>); when there are incomplete todos, it nudges the agent to continue; otherwise, a text-only response with no error signals task completion, and the loop terminates.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">If tool calls are present, the executor first performs <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">doom-loop detection</em> with a two-tier escalation: each tool call is fingerprinted as an MD5 hash of the tool name and its arguments, and fingerprints are tracked in a sliding window of the 20 most recent calls. If any fingerprint appears 3 or more times, the system injects a <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">[SYSTEM WARNING]</span> message into the conversation (e.g., “<em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p2.1.3\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">the agent has called <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p2.1.3.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">read_file</span> with the same arguments 3 times; try a different approach</em>”) and skips tool execution for that turn. If the same fingerprint recurs after the warning, the system escalates to an <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p2.1.4\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">approval-based pause</em> via the <span id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p2.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">ApprovalManager</span>, presenting the user with “<em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p2.1.6\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">Agent is repeating the same action. Allow / Break?</em>” On “Allow,” execution resumes with a one-shot guard that permits the action once before re-arming detection. On “Break,” a guidance message is injected into the conversation and the loop resets.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This two-tier approach is more robust than warnings alone: LLMs can ignore injected text, but they cannot bypass a genuine execution halt. Pre-existing safeguards (iteration caps, consecutive-read counters) are too coarse: they trigger on any repeated tool type rather than on identical <em id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">(tool, arguments)</em> pairs, and they activate only after many more iterations. Fingerprint-based detection catches stuck loops within 3 repetitions.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px5.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">When no doom loop is detected, the executor selects an execution strategy (parallel via thread pool for independent calls, sequential for dependent ones), runs the tools through the registry, and records each outcome. After execution, the results feed into the ACE memory pipeline, where a Reflector analyzes what worked and a Curator updates the playbook with new lessons for future queries. The loop then returns to Phase 0 for the next iteration.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px6\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Termination and completion detection.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px6.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px6.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The loop ends through one of four paths: the agent explicitly calls a completion tool with a summary and status (success or failure); the agent produces a text response with no tool calls and no error condition (implicit completion); the error-recovery nudge budget is exhausted (three consecutive failed attempts); or the iteration count reaches a configurable safety limit. If outstanding task items remain when the agent signals completion, the system injects additional nudges to address them before accepting termination to prevent premature completion with incomplete work. In all cases, the final conversation state is persisted to the session store.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px7\" class=\"ltx_paragraph\">\n<h5 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph\">Design evolution.</h5>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px7.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.SSS6.Px7.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Early experiments applied self-critique on every thinking output; this proved too slow for routine operations, motivating selective activation only at the HIGH thinking level. Doom-loop detection was added after observing agents repeatedly calling the same tool with identical arguments (e.g., reading a non-existent file in a loop); existing safeguards based on iteration counts and consecutive-read counters were too coarse to catch this pattern.
