generation</span></span>\n</span></td></tr>\n</table>\n</figure>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A8\" class=\"ltx_appendix\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix H </span>Intervention Case Studies</h2>\n\n<div id=\"A8.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A8.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In this section, we present the two case studies where we apply some of the tactical approaches. We also present the usage of <span id=\"A8.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> as a debugging tool, where we measure the failure modes in the system before applying any of the interventions, and then after applying the interventions we discuss below, and show that <span id=\"A8.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> can guide the intervention process as well as capture the improvements of augmentations.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"A8.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">H.1 </span>Case Study 1: AG2 - MathChat</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A8.SS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A8.SS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In this case study, we use the MathChat scenario implementation in AG2 <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib57\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">57</a>]</cite> as our baseline, where a Student agent collaborates with an Assistant agent capable of Python code execution to solve problems.\nFor benchmarking, we randomly select 200 exercises from the GSM-Plus dataset <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib81\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">81</a>]</cite>, an augmented version of GSM8K <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib82\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">82</a>]</cite> with various adversarial perturbations.\nThe first strategy is to improve the original prompt with a clear structure and a new section dedicated to the verification.\nThe detailed prompts are provided in Appendices <a href=\"#A12.SS1\" title=\"L.1 Initial prompt ‣ Appendix L AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">L.1</span></a> and <a href=\"#A12.SS2\" title=\"L.2 Structured prompt with verification section ‣ Appendix L AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">L.2</span></a>.\nThe second strategy refines the agent configuration into a more specialized system with three distinct roles:\na Problem Solver who solves the problem using a chain-of-thought approach without tools (see Appendix <a href=\"#A12.SS3\" title=\"L.3 Agent Problem Solver’s System Prompt ‣ Appendix L AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">L.3</span></a>);\na Coder who writes and executes Python code to derive the final answer (see Appendix <a href=\"#A12.SS4\" title=\"L.4 Agent Coder’s System Prompt ‣ Appendix L AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">L.4</span></a>);\na Verifier who reviews the discussion and critically evaluate the solutions, either confirming the answer or prompting further debate (see Appendix <a href=\"#A12.SS5\" title=\"L.5 Agent Verifier’s System Prompt ‣ Appendix L AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">L.5</span></a>).\nIn this setting, only the Verifier can terminate the conversation once a solution is found.\nSee Appendix <a href=\"#A12.SS6\" title=\"L.6 AG2 - MathChat: an example of conversation with three specialized agents ‣ Appendix L AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">L.6</span></a> for an example of conversation in this setting.\nTo assess the effectiveness of these strategies, we conduct benchmarking experiments across three configurations (baseline, improved prompt, and new topology) using two different LLMs (GPT-4 and GPT-4o).\nWe also perform six repetitions to evaluate the consistency of the results.\nTable <a href=\"#A8.T5\" title=\"Table 5 ‣ H.2 Case Study 2: ChatDev ‣ Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">5</span></a> summarizes the results.\nThe second column of Table <a href=\"#A8.T5\" title=\"Table 5 ‣ H.2 Case Study 2: ChatDev ‣ Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">5</span></a> show that with GPT-4, the improved prompt with verification significantly outperforms the baseline. However, the new topology does not yield the same improvement. A Wilcoxon test returned a p-value of 0.4, indicating the small gain is not statistically significant. With GPT-4o (the third column of Table <a href=\"#A8.T5\" title=\"Table 5 ‣ H.2 Case Study 2: ChatDev ‣ Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">5</span></a>), the Wilcoxon test yields a p-value of 0.03 when comparing the baseline to both the improved prompt and the new topology, indicating statistically significant improvements.\nThese results suggest that refining prompts and defining clear agent roles can reduce failures.\nHowever, these strategies are not universal, and their effectiveness varies based on factors such as the underlying LLM.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A8.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">H.2 </span>Case Study 2: ChatDev</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A8.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A8.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">ChatDev <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib5\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">5</a>]</cite> simulates a multiagent software company where different agents have different role specifications, such as a CEO, a CTO, a software engineer and a reviewer, who try to collaboratively solve a software generation task.\nIn an attempt to address the challenges we observed frequently in the traces, we implement two different interventions.\nOur first solution is refining role-specific prompts to enforce hierarchy and role adherence.\nFor instance, we observed cases where the CPO prematurely ended discussions with the CEO without fully addressing constraints.\nTo prevent this, we ensured that only superior agents can finalize conversations.\nAdditionally, we enhanced verifier role specifications to focus on task-specific edge cases.\nDetails of these interventions are in Section <a href=\"#A13\" title=\"Appendix M ChatDev Prompt Interventions ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">M</span></a>.\nThe second solution attempt involved a fundamental change to the framework’s topology.\nWe modified the framework’s topology from a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to a cyclic graph.\nThe process now terminates only when the CTO agent confirms that all reviews are properly satisfied, with a maximum iteration cutoff to prevent infinite loops.\nThis approach enables iterative refinement and more comprehensive quality assurance.\nWe test our interventions in two different benchmarks. The first one of them is a custom generated set of 32 different tasks (which we call as ProgramDev-v0, which consists of slightly different questions than the ProgamDev dataset we discussed in Section <a href=\"#S4\" title=\"4 The Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a>) where we ask the framework to generate programs ranging from “Write me a two-player chess game playable in the terminal” to ”Write me a BMI calculator”. The other benchmark is the HumanEval task of OpenAI. We report our results in Table <a href=\"#A8.T5\" title=\"Table 5 ‣ H.2 Case Study 2: ChatDev ‣ Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">5</span></a>. Notice that even though our interventions are successful in improving the performance of the framework in different tasks, they do not constitute substantial improvements, and more comprehensive solutions as we lay out in Section <a href=\"#A7.SS2\" title=\"G.2 Structural Strategies ‣ Appendix G Approaches and strategies to improve MASs ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">G.2</span></a> are required.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"A8.T5\" class=\"ltx_table\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\" in our case studies.\nThe header rows group results by strategy: AG2 and ChatDev.\nUnder AG2, GSM-Plus results are reported using GPT-4 and GPT-4o;\nunder ChatDev, results for ProgramDev and HumanEval class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">H.3 </span>Effect of the interventions on <span id=\"A8.SS3.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span></h3>\n\n<div id=\"A8.SS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A8.SS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">After carrying out the aforementioned interventions, we initially inspect the task completion rates as in Table <a href=\"#A8.T5\" title=\"Table 5 ‣ H.2 Case Study 2: ChatDev ‣ Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">5</span></a>. However, <span id=\"A8.SS3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> offers us the opportunity to look beyond the task completion rates, and we can investigate the effects of these interventions on the failure mode distribution on these MASs (AG2 and ChatDev). As illustrated in Figures <a href=\"#A8.F10\" title=\"Figure 10 ‣ H.3 Effect of the interventions on MAST ‣ Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">10</span></a> and <a href=\"#A8.F11\" title=\"Figure 11 ‣ H.3 Effect of the interventions on MAST ‣ Appendix H Intervention Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">11</span></a>, we observe that both of these interventions cause a decrease across the different failure modes observed, and it is possible to conclude that topology-based changes are more effective than prompt-based changes for both systems. Moreover, this displays another usage of <span id=\"A8.SS3.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span>, which is as well as an analysis tool after execution, it can serve as a debugging tool for future improvements as it shows which failure modes particular augmentations to the system can solve or miss, guiding future intervention decisions.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"A8.F10\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><object type=\"image/svg+xml\" data=\"2503.13657v3/intervention_comparison_threeway_ag2_system_design.svg\" id=\"A8.F10.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:429/170;\" width=\"429\" height=\"170\"></object>\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\">Figure 10: </span>Effect of prompt and topology interventions on AG2 as captured by <span id=\"A8.F10.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> using the automated LLM-as-a-Judge</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<figure id=\"A8.F11\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><object type=\"image/svg+xml\" data=\"2503.13657v3/intervention_comparison_threeway_chatdev_system_design.svg\" ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> using the automated LLM-as-a-Judge</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<div class=\"ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage\"></div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A9\" class=\"ltx_appendix\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix I </span>Analysis on Multi-Agent Systems with Open-Source Models</h2>\n\n<div id=\"A9.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A9.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In this section, we also provide the analysis of failure modes on MetaGPT and ChatDev frameworks where the underlying LLMs are open-source models. In particular, we chose to use <code id=\"A9.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter\">Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct</code> <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib83\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">83</a>]</cite> and <code id=\"A9.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter\">CodeLlama-7b-Instruct-hf</code> <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib84\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">84</a>]</cite> models for these two frameworks. The analysis of failure modes is shown in Table <a href=\"#A9.T6\" title=\"Table 6 ‣ Appendix I Analysis on Multi-Agent Systems with Open-Source Models ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">6</span></a>. This new analysis reveals two key findings:</p>\n<ul id=\"A9.I1\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"A9.I1.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A9.I1.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A9.I1.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">There is a significant performance difference between the two open-source models. <code id=\"A9.I1.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter\">Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct</code> is substantially more robust than <code id=\"A9.I1.i1.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter\">CodeLlama-7b-Instruct-hf</code> on these tasks, exhibiting far fewer failures overall.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A9.I1.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A9.I1.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A9.I1.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Both open-source models show a higher frequency of failures compared to the leading closed-source models analyzed in our paper (GPT-4o and Claude-3). This suggests a performance gap and highlights important areas for future improvement in open-source models for multi-agent tasks.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"A9.T6\" class=\"ltx_table\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\" style=\"font-size:90%;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_table\">Table 6: </span>Failure Mode Occurrences in 400 Traces with Open-Source Models. class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix J </span>Correlation of Failure Modes with Different Statistics</h2>\n\n<div id=\"A10.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A10.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In this section, we provide how the failure modes in <span id=\"A10.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold\">MAST</span> correlate with some important statistics, such as the actual task completion rates, and different benchmarks.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"A10.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">J.1 </span>How Indicative are Different Failure Modes of Actual Success?</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A10.SS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A10.SS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">One important question to ask is, for traces where we know whether they succeeded or failed and if we do not provide the success or failure result to the LLM Annotator, how do different failure modes correlate with actual task success and failures? In particular, we want to measure how indicative of the failure modes given by the LLM Annotator on actual task completions. The analysis on ChatDev and MetaGPT are provided in Table <a href=\"#A10.T7\" title=\"Table 7 ‣ J.1 How Indicative are Different Failure Modes of Actual Success? ‣ Appendix J Correlation of Failure Modes with Different Statistics ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">7</span></a>. This new analysis reveals three key findings:</p>\n<ul id=\"A10.I1\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"A10.I1.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A10.I1.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A10.I1.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Successful runs are not failure-free. Our results show that failures occur in both successful and failed traces, but failed traces have a higher overall frequency of failures. This confirms that a higher number of failures do signal a higher chance of final task failure.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A10.I1.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A10.I1.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A10.I1.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Some failures are more ”fatal” than others. The data shows a clear distinction between failure types. Certain failures, such as 1.5 Unaware of Termination Conditions and 2.4 Information Withholding, appear almost exclusively in failed runs, suggesting they are critical bugs that are highly likely to derail the task.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A10.I1.i3\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A10.I1.i3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A10.I1.i3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Some failures are non-fatal. In contrast, verification-related failures like 3.2 No or Incomplete Verification and 3.3 Incorrect Verification appear frequently even in successful runs. This suggests that while these systems can complete some tasks, their verification process still contains flaws. MAST identifies such systemic weaknesses, even when they do not cause an immediate task failure.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"A10.T7\" class=\"ltx_table\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\" style=\"font-size:90%;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_table\">Table 7: </span>Failure mode occurrence rates for ChatDev and MetaGPT on successful and unsuccessful
